Exam Blueprint & Grading

Dr. Doan answered the "how is this graded" questions at the end of the session. Two facts drive how you should study: the weeks are balanced, not weighted, and each half of the written exam has its own 70% floor.

ItemWhat she saidStudy consequence
Total questions115 on the first written examRoughly 6 questions per study-guide objective area.
Split~56 OMM/OPP tagged, ~64 clinical skills (Patient Care) tagged; some are double-tagged because special tests are taught in both coursesSpecial tests are worth double. Learn them once, get credit twice.
Week weighting"No, I balanced them." W1 through W7 are evenDo not gamble on skipping a week.
Week 8Week 8 #1 (diagnosis + treatment techniques) overlaps every other week — "there are a lot of questions on number 1 in week 8"The technique chart and the diagnosis/naming rules are the single highest-yield block on the exam.
Guaranteed questionsExplicitly promised: TART acute vs chronic, barriers, Fryette Type I/II, inhaled vs exhaled ribs + muscle energy, the 5 modelsThese five are non-negotiable. Get them to automatic.
Written pass mark70% overallBelow 70% overall → retake the whole test; a pass on retake caps your grade at 70%.
Half-test ruleOverall ≥70% but either half (OMM-tagged or Patient-Care-tagged) <70% → retake that halfRetaking a half does not raise your grade. It is a competency gate only.
Course pass mark75% overall course gradeScraping 70% on every written will leave the course grade under 75%. 70% is survival, not a target.
Practical (skills/PE/CSA)75% required, and they can cap the line/sectionDifferent floor than the written — don't mix them up.

⚠ Caveat

Those weights were read aloud mid-sentence and sum to about 90%, so at least one line is missing or garbled in the recording. The syllabus grading table at the back of the Brightspace syllabus is the authority — she said so explicitly.

🔑 Her actual tell for what's tested

"If I say there's a question on TART, there's a question on TART. If I say there's a question on barriers, there's a question on barriers." Every time she said "there is a question on X" in this session, X is on the exam. Every one of those is flagged in this document with a ⭐ PROMISED pill.

Q: You score 78% overall on the written but 66% on the OMM-tagged half. What happens?

Answer

You retake the OMM half only. You must show ≥70% on it, but your 78% does not change. The half-test retake is a competency gate, not a grade repair.

Week 1 · LO 1
Case vignette

Clinical reasoning lens ⭐ PROMISED

The Five Osteopathic Models

Dr. Doan opened with these because "you will see a question on our exam" and they show up on COMLEX. The question format is always the same: a case vignette gives you a clue, and you name the model — or you're given the model and asked which treatment fits.

🧠 Memory Hook — the five models

"Big Rusty Nails Move Bones" → Biomechanical · Respiratory-circulatory · Neurologic · Metabolic-energetic · Behavioral.

ModelThe vignette clue that gives it awayGoal of treatmentClassic OMT example
BiomechanicalPosture, motion, gait, ambulation, structural asymmetry, "he limps," alignmentRestore useful motion and postural/anatomic reliability so tissue works with less mechanical dragME, HVLA, articulatory, Still, BLT to restore segmental/joint motion
Respiratory / CirculatoryArteries, veins, lymphatics, diffusion, "breathe better," edema, JVD, congestion, waste removalOptimize arterial supply, venous/lymphatic return, and diaphragm pressure gradientsThoracic inlet/outlet, diaphragm doming, lymphatic pump, rib raising, pedal pump
NeurologicNeuroendocrine-immune function, autonomic tone, facilitation, nociception, viscerosomatic reflexesReduce facilitation and rebalance sympathetic/parasympathetic toneRib raising — she called this out by name: on licensing exams rib raising is scored as a neurologic treatment because it reduces sympathetic tone. Also Chapman's points, suboccipital release (vagal)
Metabolic / EnergeticEfficiency, energy conservation, "the work of breathing/walking," allostatic load, nutritional/metabolic processesReduce the energy cost the body is paying to compensateGentle, efficient techniques chosen for a patient with low reserve; remove dysfunctions that force extra effort
BehavioralPsychosocial, education, spiritual, coping, lifestyle change, smoking/alcohol, caregiver stress, adherenceMaximize coping capability and healthy lifestyle adaptationCounseling, HEP, smoking cessation, safety planning, follow-up, realistic goal setting
🩺 The Week 1 anchor case

67-year-old man, acute right ankle sprain, COPD, worsening dyspnea/orthopnea/edema, diastolic heart failure, smoking, alcohol, caregiver stress. Ask five questions about him, not one:

  • Resp/Circ — 1 cm diaphragmatic excursion, JVD, edema → venous/lymph return is the target: thoracic inlet, ribs, respiratory diaphragm, pelvic diaphragm.
  • Biomechanical — right posterior fibular head + internally rotated navicular/cuboid → antalgic gait.
  • Neurologic — T4 and T5–T8 findings + ATFL tenderness → viscerosomatic and nociceptive input maintaining facilitation.
  • Metabolic — a limp plus tachypnea is expensive; in COPD/HF that is not trivial.
  • Behavioral — smoking, alcohol, and his role as his wife's caregiver.

Q: A vignette describes rib raising performed to reduce sympathetic hyperactivity in a patient with pancreatitis. Which osteopathic model is this treatment best classified under?

Answer

Neurologic. Dr. Doan flagged this specifically: rib raising is mechanically a rib technique, but on licensing exams it is classified as a neurologic-model treatment because its purpose is reducing sympathetic tone.

Q: A vignette emphasizes that treatment is aimed at helping the body conserve energy and improve the efficiency of metabolic and nutritional processes. Which model?

Answer

Metabolic/energetic. The tell is the word efficiency or energy conservation. If the same sentence had said "posture and motion," it would be biomechanical.

Week 8 throwback
First-year review

Somatic dysfunction ⭐ PROMISED

TART — Acute vs Chronic

"I know you all know that, but you don't think about it all the time." This is a guaranteed question and it is almost always framed as acute versus chronic tissue texture change.

🧠 Memory Hook — TART

T·A·R·T = Tissue texture change · Asymmetry · Restriction of motion · Tenderness.
And for the acute/chronic split: "Acute is Angry & Wet. Chronic is Cold & Ropey."

TART elementACUTECHRONIC
Tissue textureErythema / redness, boggy, edematous, moist, warm, hypertonic — increased tone, spasmPale, cool, dry, flaccid, ropey, fibrotic, decreased muscle tone, no erythema
AsymmetryPresentPresent, but the body is partially compensated
RestrictionPresent; painful with movementStill present, but often decreased because of partial adaptation
TendernessSharp and severeDull and achy, or minimal
VasomotorIncreased blood flow, heat, erythemaDecreased blood flow, coolness, no erythema
🔑 The trap

Chronic does not mean "no findings." Chronic still has asymmetry and restriction — the difference is quality (ropey/fibrotic vs boggy/edematous) and degree (partially compensated, less pain). A stem that says "cool, dry, ropey tissue with mild dull aching" is chronic even though every TART letter is still positive.

Q: Palpation reveals a warm, boggy, moist paraspinal region with increased muscle tone, marked restriction, and sharp tenderness. Acute or chronic, and what does that tell you about technique choice?

Answer

Acute. Boggy + moist + warm + hypertonic + sharp pain is the acute signature. Practically, acute dysfunction usually gets more frequent, gentler treatment — indirect techniques (counterstrain, FPR, BLT) are better tolerated than forcing a direct barrier through an angry, guarding tissue.

Week 8 throwback
Week 2 · LO 5

Barrier concepts ⭐ PROMISED

Barriers

"Barriers is another throwback that's going to show up... If you get a barrier question, it shows up on licensing boards." Know the diagram and know how to apply it to a technique.

BarrierDefinitionWhat lies beyond itTechnique relationship
Physiologic barrierLimit of active range of motion — as far as the patient can move themselvesThe elastic range (passive motion)Never exceed it, in any technique
Elastic barrierThe range between physiologic and anatomic — what the physician can take the joint through passivelyThe anatomic barrierThis is where HVLA's thrust and cavitation happen
Anatomic barrierLimit of passive motion, set by bone/ligament structureTissue failure — joint disruption, tissue/tendon/ligament tearing, bony injuryNever a target. Beyond it is injury
Restrictive / pathologic barrierA functional limit encountered within the normal active range of motionStill normal range that the patient cannot accessDirect techniques engage it; indirect techniques move away from it
Neutral / idlingFacets neither opened nor closed; tissue free to move in every direction—FPR's starting position; Still passes through it on the way to the barrier
Position of easeDirection where tissue softens and resistance decreases—Counterstrain and FPR end here; Still starts here
🧠 Memory Hook — barrier order

Moving outward from midline: "P → E → A" — Physiologic (active) → Elastic (passive) → Anatomic (structure). Think "PEA in a pod", and the restrictive barrier is a pebble inside the pod — it crowds the space before you ever reach P.

And for permanence: "Restrictive can become permanent." A pathologic barrier can become a fixed restriction if the underlying pathologic change persists.

🧭 Applying barriers to a technique question

A barrier question is usually disguised as a technique question. Convert it: "the physician engages the restrictive barrier and the patient contracts against resistance" = direct + active = muscle energy. "The physician positions away from the barrier into ease and holds 90 seconds" = indirect + passive = counterstrain. "Positions at the barrier and thrusts through it" = direct + passive = HVLA.

Q: Which barrier represents the limit of passive motion, beyond which tissue disruption occurs?

Answer

The anatomic barrier. Beyond it you get joint disruption and ligament/tendon/bony injury. The physiologic barrier is the limit of active motion — that's the pair most commonly swapped in a distractor.

Week 1 · LO 3–4
Week 8 throwback

Fryette's principles & regional mechanics ⭐ PROMISED

Fryette Type I, II, III & Naming

She called them "Fryette's principles" and warned you may see them written that way instead of "Type 1 and Type 2." "You have to know these down pat." Students were still confused about them in second year — do not be one of them.

1️⃣

Type I — Neutral, Opposite, Group

  • Spine is in neutral — no flexion or extension
  • Sidebending and rotation occur to opposite sides
  • Involves a group of vertebrae
  • Documented e.g. T5–T8 N SR RL — neutral, sidebent right, rotated left
  • Treat the middle of the group — she said this explicitly
2️⃣

Type II — Non-neutral, Same, Single

  • Spine is in a non-neutral position — flexed or extended
  • Rotation and sidebending occur to the same side
  • Single vertebral segment
  • Documented F SR RR (or FRSR) / E SR RR (ERSR)
3️⃣

Type III — Newton, not really Fryette

  • Not truly Fryette's — it comes from Newton's third law
  • Motion introduced in one plane reduces range of motion in the other planes
  • "For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction" applied to the spine
  • You will occasionally see it on questions
🧠 Memory Hook — Type I vs Type II

Type 1 = "N-O-G" → Neutral · Opposite · Group.
Type 2 = "two S's, and 2 is the number of letters that match" → Same side · Single segment (and it's non-neutral: flexed or extended).
Faster still: "1 is Odd → Opposite. 2 is Same → Same side, Single."

🔑 The rule underneath everything

Somatic dysfunctions are always named for the FREEDOM of motion, never the restriction. "We're naming things on the way and where they are." Every naming question resolves if you hold this.

Regional mechanics atlas — where Type I and Type II live

RegionMechanicsHow it's namedThe catch
OA (C0–C1)Acts like Type I — sidebending and rotation are always oppositeOA N/F/E SR RLOA can be neutral, flexed, or extended — but S and R are opposite regardless. Diagnose with a tiny translatory motion at the occiput; do not sidebend the whole neck.
AA (C1–C2)Rotation only. No flexion, extension, or sidebending diagnosisAA RR or AA RLTested at 45° of flexion to lock out the lower cervicals. About half of all cervical rotation happens here. "It's kind of its own special case."
C2–C7Typical cervicals — follow Type II: sidebending and rotation same sideC4 F SR RR or C5 E SL RLNot true Fryette mechanics — the uncovertebral joints of Luschka force the coupling. Diagnose on the articular pillars, not the sharp transverse processes. Screen all the way to C7.
T1–L5Can be either Type I or Type II, and both can coexist in the same spineT4 E SR RR, T7–T9 N SL RR, L1 F SL RLShe gave the example of a neutral group T7–T9 with a Type II segment sitting below it. A patient with a bigger AP flexion/extension curve is more likely to show a Type II pattern.
🧠 Memory Hook — cervical mechanics

"OA = Opposite Always. AA = All About rotation. C2–C7 = Copy (same side)."
And for AA testing: "45 to lock the rest" — flex to 45° so only C1–C2 can rotate.

Three-position diagnosis — how you actually get to a name

  1. NeutralFind the posterior transverse process, or the sidebending restriction. That side gives you rotation.
  2. FlexionDoes the asymmetry improve? If yes → the segment is flexed.
  3. ExtensionDoes the asymmetry improve? If yes → the segment is extended.
  4. No meaningful change?It's a neutral Type I — check whether neighbouring segments share the pattern, making it a group curve.
🩺 Worked examples
  • Right TP of L4 posterior; more symmetric in flexion, worse in extension → L4 F SR RR.
  • T5–T8 with left TPs posterior and no change in flexion or extension → T5–T8 N SR RL.
  • Occiput sidebends more freely right, improves in extension, worse in flexion → OA E SR RL.
  • AA rotates more freely right → AA RR.

Spinal landmarks — "really good to know" (from Savarese)

LandmarkLevel
Suprasternal (jugular) notchT2
Spine of the scapulaT3
Sternal angle / angle of LouisT4
Nipple (dermatome)T4
Inferior angle of the scapulaT7
Xiphoid processT9
UmbilicusT10
Aortic hiatusT12
Iliac crestL4–L5
🧠 Memory Hook — landmarks ladder

2-3-4 up top (notch, scapular spine, angle of Louis + nipple) · 7-9-10 down the middle (scapula tip, xiphoid, umbilicus) · 12 = aorta leaves · L4 = crest.

Nerve root exit rules

RegionRuleExam application
Cervical8 cervical nerve roots. The upper 7 exit above their same-numbered vertebra; C8 exits below C7A C5–C6 disc affects the C6 root cervically. The numbering flips after C7.
Brachial plexusC5 – T1Thoracic outlet syndrome and brachial plexus traction injuries.
LumbarRoots exit at the intervertebral foramen of the lowest corresponding vertebra — L4 exits between L4 and L5A posterolateral L4–L5 disc typically catches the traversing L5 root; a far-lateral herniation catches the exiting L4.
Cord terminationSpinal cord ends at L1–L2 (conus medullaris)Below that is cauda equina — hence the syndrome.
Lumbar main motionFlexion / extensionWhy extension-based pain suggests facet/stenosis and flexion-based pain suggests disc.

Q: On seated screening, T6, T7 and T8 all have prominent left transverse processes. The asymmetry is unchanged in flexion and in extension. Name the dysfunction and state where you would treat it.

Answer

T6–T8 N SR RL — a Type I group curve (neutral, group, sidebending and rotation opposite; left posterior TPs mean rotated left, so sidebent right). Because it's a Type I group, you treat the middle of the group — T7.

Q: The OA is diagnosed as sidebent left. Which way is it rotated, and why can you answer that instantly?

Answer

Rotated right. At the OA, sidebending and rotation are always opposite, regardless of whether the joint is neutral, flexed, or extended. That is the one thing the OA never violates.

Week 8 · LO 1
Highest-yield block on the exam

"Dr. Doan's chart" ⭐ PROMISED — multiple questions

The Master Technique Chart

This is the slide she said she built herself — "there's a partial chart like this in the Savarese book, but it's not complete in Savarese's new edition." She spent the most time here and said flatly: "there are multiple questions on these topics."

🔑 Four things you must know for EVERY technique
  1. Active or passive?Is the patient helping you — moving a limb, purposeful breathing, holding their breath, deep inspirations/expirations? That's active. Just lying there relaxed and breathing normally? Passive.
  2. Direct or indirect?Direct engages the restrictive barrier. Indirect moves away from the barrier, into the direction of ease. Some techniques can be either.
  3. The steps, force, and angle.The exact sequence, what force you apply, and in what direction.
  4. How long do you hold it?3–5 sec? 10? 20? 30? 60? 90? Or not at all? "How long do you hold it, or do you not hold it at all?"

Plus: contraindications to the technique you're choosing.

The chart

Quiz this table with the toolbar above it — hide the Direct/Indirect and Hold columns first, then shuffle the rows.

TechniqueDirect / IndirectPatient Active / PassiveHold timeRecipe in one line
Facilitated Positional Release (FPR)
Dr. Frothingham		 INDIRECT only PASSIVE only 3–5 sec (5 is better) Start neutral → apply facilitating force (compression, torsion, or traction) → move into ease → hold 3–5 sec → release → return to neutral → recheck
Still Technique
Dr. Frothingham		 DIRECT (combined indirect→direct) PASSIVE No hold — "there's no time anymore" Start at ease → apply facilitating force (compression or traction) → move smoothly through neutral all the way to the restrictive barrier → return to neutral → recheck
Balanced Ligamentous Tension (BLT)
Dr. Edwards		 BOTH — exaggeration and direct action ACTIVE or PASSIVE
At UNE, usually taught active		 10 sec minimum; often 20–30 sec or more Disengage (distraction or compression) → exaggerate toward ease → balance in all directions → direct action back toward anatomic neutral → wait for release → return & recheck
Soft Tissue
Dr. Yi		 DIRECT only PASSIVE only Rhythmic / sustained; no fixed count Engage the musculature underneath the fascia — deeper than fascia. Linear and longitudinal stretching, kneading, bowstringing, inhibition, traction

Dr. Yi		 DIRECT or INDIRECT ACTIVE or PASSIVE 20–30 sec, sometimes 60 — usually 30–60 Engage the fascia (the outer wrapping) toward bind or ease → hold → follow it into unwinding through every direction it wants to go → stop when it stops creeping → return & recheck
Counterstrain (Strain-Counterstrain) INDIRECT PASSIVE 90 seconds Find the most tender point → keep your finger on it → establish a 0–10 tenderness scale → position of ease until tenderness drops to ≤3/10 → hold 90 sec → physician passively returns patient to neutral → recheck the same point
Muscle Energy (ME) DIRECT ACTIVE 3–5 sec × 3–5 repetitions Position at the restrictive barrier → patient pushes against physician's unyielding counterforce 3–5 sec → patient fully relaxes → engage the new barrier → repeat 3–5× → return to neutral → recheck
HVLA DIRECT PASSIVE Instantaneous thrust — no hold Position against the barrier → high-velocity, low-amplitude thrust through the restrictive barrier → return to neutral → recheck
Articulatory DIRECT PASSIVE Repeated cycles; no single hold Position against the barrier → low-velocity, moderate-to-high amplitude springing repeatedly through the restrictive barrier → return & recheck. Springing, not a thrust

🧠 Memory Hook — the club memberships

Pure INDIRECT club: "CS + FPR" — Counterstrain and FPR. Only two members, both passive.
Pure DIRECT + PASSIVE club: "HAS-S" — HVLA, Articulatory, Soft tissue, Still.
Only DIRECT + ACTIVE: Muscle Energy — it's the one that needs the patient to push.
The "anything goes" club: "MBC" — MFR, BLT, Cranial. Direct or indirect, active or passive.

🧠 Memory Hook — the hold-time ladder

3 → 30 → 90
3–5 sec = FPR hold, and ME contraction.
10–30+ sec = BLT balancing.
20–60 sec (usually 30–60) = MFR unwinding.
90 sec = Counterstrain, every time.
Zero = Still, HVLA. Still has no hold time anymore; HVLA is a thrust.

🧭 The compare-and-contrast question format

She described the exact question types to expect:

  • "Which of the following recipes of steps is the correct one?" — sequence questions for FPR, Still, BLT.
  • "Which techniques are direct and passive / indirect and passive / can be both?" — matching or multi-select.
  • A regional twist: "The patient will be treated with BLT for the clavicle / the fibula. What are the steps?" — the recipe is the same, but the setup detail changes.
  • Given a described technique in a vignette, name it.

Q: A physician places a hypertonic cervical segment in a neutral position, applies gentle compression through the top of the head, moves the segment into its position of ease, holds for five seconds, then returns the patient to neutral. Name the technique, and classify it.

Answer

Facilitated Positional Release (FPR) — indirect and passive. The giveaway sequence is neutral → force → ease. If the stem had started in the position of ease and ended at the barrier, it would be Still.

Q: Which of the following techniques can be performed as either direct or indirect AND with the patient either active or passive? (Select all that apply.) A. Counterstrain · B. Myofascial release · C. HVLA · D. Balanced ligamentous tension · E. Muscle energy

Answer

B (MFR) and D (BLT). Counterstrain is indirect/passive only. HVLA is direct/passive only. Muscle energy is direct/active only. Cranial would also belong in this group, but it isn't tested on this exam.

Q: A physician contacts a joint, springs it rhythmically through the restrictive barrier a dozen times at low velocity and moderate amplitude, then rechecks. Still technique or articulatory?

Answer

Articulatory. Two tells: (1) it never started in the position of ease, and (2) it uses repeated springing rather than one smooth arc. Still starts in ease, adds a facilitating force, and makes one arc through neutral to the barrier.

Week 2 · LO 1–6, 11
New technique

Dr. Frothingham ⭐ PROMISED — compare & contrast

FPR & Still Technique

"There are questions on comparing and contrasting FPR and Still... If you see these techniques in a question, be able to identify which is an FPR sequence and which is a Still sequence."

FPR — the neutral / "idling" starting position

Still — ease, facilitating force, then direct arc to the barrier

🅕

FPR — Neutral → Force → Ease

  1. Diagnose & monitorName the dysfunction; keep a palpating finger on the segment / tender tissue / AGR.
  2. Place in neutral / idlingFacets neither opened nor closed. In the cervical spine, flex down to the level to create idling.
  3. Add facilitating forceUsually gentle compression (or torsion). Use traction if compression isn't tolerated.
  4. Move into easePosition into the freedom of motion — this is the indirect component.
  5. Hold 3–5 sec, return, recheckPassively return to anatomic neutral, repeat if needed, reassess TART/motion.

Classification: indirect, passive, only.

🅢

Still — Ease → Force → Barrier

  1. DiagnoseName the segment/region and identify the position of ease.
  2. Start in easeUsually exaggerate the diagnosed position. C5 ERSL starts in ERSL.
  3. Add facilitating forceCompression is common; traction/distraction is allowed and often better tolerated.
  4. Move through neutral to the barrierOne smooth arc. Do not exceed physiologic ROM.
  5. Return & recheckPassively return to neutral, repeat if needed, recheck motion/TART.

Classification: passive; considered direct because it ends at the barrier. No hold time.

🧠 Memory Hook — FPR vs Still, one line each

FPR = "Flat, Push, Rest." Flatten to neutral, push (compress), rest into ease for 3–5 sec.
Still = "STarts In ease, Leaves at the Limit." The name itself carries the order.
Or purely mechanically: FPR ends where Still begins.

FPR vs Counterstrain — the other compare-and-contrast

FeatureFPRStrain-Counterstrain
Basic typePassive, indirectPassive, indirect
What you monitorThe diagnosed segment / tissue / AGRThe tender point and the patient's reported tenderness
Starting setupNeutral / idling firstStraight to the position of comfort for that tender point
Added forceYes — compression, torsion, or tractionNo required added compressive force
Hold3–5 seconds90 seconds
Vignette discriminator"Neutral → force → ease""Tender point → ease → tenderness drops"

Still vs Articulatory

FeatureStillArticulatory
TypePassive, combined indirect→directPassive, direct
Starting positionPosition of easeNo requirement to start in ease
Facilitating forceRequired — compression or traction before the arcNot required
MotionOne smooth arc through neutral to the barrierRepeated rhythmic springing through the barrier
Velocity / amplitudeSingle controlled arcLow velocity, moderate-to-high amplitude

Indications & contraindications for FPR and Still

Her verdict: "FPR is one of the safest techniques you could possibly use" because you're taking the person into the position of ease. Still is fairly safe too, but it ends at a restriction — "you might think a second time about Still."

✅ Indications

  • Hypertonic muscles — superficial group curves or deep segmental dysfunction
  • Fascial restrictions
  • Patients with limited motion who tolerate low-force positioning
  • Somatic dysfunction with restricted motion, TART, or a local AGR
  • Osteoporosis is fine for FPR — she said so explicitly: it's not a direct technique

⚠ Contraindications / cautions

  • Patient cannot tolerate the treatment position, or refuses
  • Cervical radiculopathy — a caution, not an absolute
  • Joint pathology in secondary areas
  • Recent trauma
  • Unstable joints, severe osteoporosis (for Still's direct phase), malignancy, infection, severe rheumatologic disease, congenital instability, stenosis
  • Region-specific: hip replacement can contraindicate some lumbar leg-sweep setups
🧭 Proposed mechanism of action

FPR: shortens the involved muscle spindles → decreases gamma efferent gain → lowers Ia afferent excitation → reduces extrafusal muscle tone. Practical implication: don't fight the tone, shorten and quiet it.
Still: uses the same proposed neurophysiologic relaxation, then adds a direct mobilizing arc through neutral toward the barrier.

Regional application — FPR and Still by region

RegionDiagnosis ruleFPRStill
OASidebending & rotation opposite; named OA F/E Sx RyNeutralize OA, gentle force, move into OA ease 3–5 secStart in OA ease, add force, carry toward the opposite barrier
AARotation only; AA RR or AA RLNeutral upper-cervical setup, gentle force, rotate briefly toward easeStart rotated into ease, compress, rotate through the restrictive barrier
Lower cervicalC2–C7 usually Type II; S & R same sideFlex to neutral/idling at the level, compress, move into ease (C5 ERSL → neutral, compress, ease into ERSL)Start in ease/diagnosis, compress, move opposite: C5 ERSL → toward FRSR
Thoracic Type INeutral group curve; S & R oppositeReduce kyphosis to neutral, compress, move the group into freedomStart in the group-curve ease, compress through torso, carry to the opposite barrier
Thoracic Type IISingle segment F/E; S & R same sideSit up to neutral, compress, position F/E + S/R into easeStart in the diagnosis/ease, compress, move to opposite F/E and opposite S/R
Lumbar Type IISupine; prominent TP gives rotation. Adduction = flexion, abduction = extensionConceptual — Week 2 lab emphasized Still for lumbarUse the lower extremity: start in flexion or extension ease, add compression/traction, sweep through the opposite arc
Anterior / posterior ribMechanical (non-physiologic) subluxationNot the Week 2 emphasis for mechanical ribsMonitor the rib angle, find ipsilateral arm ease, compress toward the rib, move the arm through the opposite arc to the barrier

OA = the "yes" joint · AA = the "no" joint

Lower cervical coupling — sidebending and rotation to the SAME side

Screening & the Area of Greatest Resistance (AGR)

Screening is not diagnosis — it finds where motion is worst fastest. Then you fully diagnose the AGR region rather than every normal-moving level.

RegionSetupMotion testedWhat you record
Head / OASeated; physician cradles occiput/headSide-slip right and left at the occiputSide-to-side restriction (AA is better diagnosed supine)
CervicalStabilize head with one hand, contact each segment with the otherTranslate each segment laterally R/L from upper cervicals to C7Segment with greatest asymmetry/resistance
ThoracicOne hand on shoulder, other just lateral to the spinous processesInferior/medial compression through the shoulder to induce segmental motionThoracic segment or group-curve AGR
RibsSame seated setup; monitoring hand moves laterally to the rib anglesRib angle motion/prominence level by levelRib AGR — and whether the ribs or the thoracic spine feel worse

Seated cervical segmental translation R/L

Rib angle screen compared against thoracic segmental findings

🔑 The thoracic-before-rib rule, in screening form

Dr. Stevens brought this up again the same day: "if you think you have a posterior rib, you might not have a posterior rib." You may have a thoracic problem next to it — and treating the thoracic segment makes the "posterior rib" disappear, because the rib is just following a rotated vertebra through the costotransverse ligament. Check the vertebra first. A true mechanical rib dysfunction is more likely after trauma and has sharp, discrete "ice-pick" pain.

Q: C5 is diagnosed as ERSL. Describe the Still treatment arc, and contrast it with the FPR setup for the same segment.

Answer

Still: start in the ease — ERSL — add compression, then carry the segment in one smooth arc through neutral toward the opposite barrier, classically FRSR. No hold; return and recheck.

FPR: start by flexing to neutral/idling at C5, add compression, then move into the ease (ERSL), hold 3–5 seconds, return to neutral, recheck. The difference is entirely the order of operations.

Q: A patient with severe osteoporosis has a painful, hypertonic upper thoracic segment. Which of FPR, Still, or HVLA is the safest first choice and why?

Answer

FPR. Dr. Doan said this directly: you can do FPR on someone with osteoporosis because it is indirect and passive — you never engage the restrictive barrier. Still has a direct end-phase, so think twice. HVLA is contraindicated at a joint with osteoporosis.

Week 4 · LO 1–8
New technique

Dr. Edwards ⭐ PROMISED — "know your recipe"

Balanced Ligamentous Tension

She was asked directly for an example BLT question and gave three: the steps of BLT ("a real common question"), BLT for the clavicle, and BLT for the fibula. "The recipe is the same, but it might be just slightly different on how you do the technique depending on where it is in the body."

🔑 History & definition

Originally described by William Garner Sutherland, published as The Osteopathic Technique of Wm. G. Sutherland in the 1949 Yearbook of the Academy of Applied Osteopathy.

Definition: a technique for articular somatic dysfunction in which the physician creates a stable fulcrum and positions the joint at the point where ligamentous tensions are minimized, allowing the patient's inherent physiologic forces to activate the release.

Mechanism in one sentence: counterbalance the tissue strain until the dysfunctional area is reconnected with the body's constant inherent motion, then let the patient's own forces reposition the strain.

The BLT recipe from the course deck

Mechanisms of leverage — exaggeration, direct action, disengagement

The recipe — this is the question she predicted

  1. DisengageSeparate the opposing joint surfaces. Either distraction (pulling) or compression — whichever gives you wiggle room to work with that ligament.
  2. Exaggerate toward easeMove slightly farther in the same direction as the strain pattern to relax the ligaments. You are not taking it all the way to the ease — you're moving toward it, because you're balancing the whole time.
  3. Balance in all directions"Does it go better this way or that way?" Test every plane, find where each moves easier, and stack — or balance one plane at a time.
  4. Direct action toward anatomic neutralOnce it's loosening, move back toward where the joint should have been. Moving toward anatomic neutral is the direct-action component.
  5. Add respiratory / postural cooperationThe patient may hold a breath phase, change posture, or move a limb — or do nothing at all.
  6. Wait for releaseSome tissue response by ~10 seconds; complete release often 20–30 seconds or more. Use palpatory feedback, not a stopwatch.
  7. Return to neutral & recheckReassess the original finding.
🧠 Memory Hook — the BLT recipe

"DEB-DR" → Disengage · Exaggerate · Balance · Direct action · Release & recheck.
Or the leverage triad on its own: "DED" — Disengagement, Exaggeration, Direct action. Those three words are the vocabulary LO.

The four vocabulary terms (LO 4 — expect a definition-matching question)

TermDefinitionExampleWhy BLT uses it
ExaggerationMove the joint slightly farther in the same direction as the strain patternAA rotated right is gently taken farther into right rotationGoing with the tissue preference decreases net tissue tension
Direct actionMove the joint back toward its normal / anatomic neutral positionAA rotated right is moved left, toward neutralMay be the balance in one plane while another plane uses exaggeration
DisengagementSeparate opposing joint surfaces — usually traction, sometimes compression — before securing the balanceGently distracting the rib head, SI joint, fibula, or occipital condylesReduces compression and gives the joint room to balance
Inherent forcesAny physiologic force or motion occurring within the bodyRespiration, fluid-pressure shifts, posture, involuntary rhythmsThese are the activating forces once the fulcrum is set — BLT adds no thrust and no muscle contraction
🧬 Why BLT doesn't fit the direct/indirect boxes

The point of best balance can involve exaggeration in one plane, direct action in another, and disengagement layered underneath both. That's why the chart lists it as both. If a question forces a single answer, look at what the stem emphasizes: "balanced tension, fulcrum, inherent forces, waiting for release" → BLT.

Respiratory vs postural cooperation (LO 5)

Cooperation typeBest fitHow to use itExamples
RespiratoryAxial skeleton and regions strongly moved by breathPatient inhales/exhales; note which phase gives greatest ease; ask them to hold that phase until air hunger; fine-tuneRibs, thoracic inlet/outlet, OA, SI when breath clearly helps
PosturalAppendicular skeleton / extremitiesAsk for slow limb motion; stop where balance improves; patient holds while you monitor releaseFibula with dorsiflexion/plantarflexion or foot external rotation; SI with hip IR/ER or an ankle prop
CombinedJunctional or large articular regionsStack the most helpful posture and the best respiratory phase, then fine-tuneSI joint using both hip rotation and a breath phase
🧠 Memory Hook — which cooperation?

"Axial breathes, Limbs move." Respiratory cooperation for the axial skeleton; postural cooperation for the extremities.

Indications & contraindications

✅ Indications

  • Acutely tender dysfunctions where direct barrier engagement is poorly tolerated
  • Geriatric, osteoporotic, delicate, pediatric, and hospitalized patients
  • Articular somatic dysfunction anywhere a ligamentous articular mechanism can be contacted
  • Regions where thrust, strong muscle contraction, or repeated articulation is undesirable

⚠ Contraindications

  • Lack of consent
  • Patient intolerance of the treatment positioning
  • Actual or suspected fracture in the tissue being steered — "this technique works with ligaments and joints"
  • Severe instability, infection, malignancy, acute vascular/neurologic red flags
⚠ Gentle ≠ risk-free

BLT uses less force than most direct techniques, but it still moves and tensions tissue. If the structure may be fractured or unstable, do not steer it.

BLT vs FPR vs Still — the three-way table

FeatureBLTFPRStill
Core ideaBalance ligamentous/articular tension around a fulcrum; let inherent forces correctNeutral/idling + facilitating force, then indirect easeIndirect ease + compression/traction, then a direct arc through the barrier
Starting emphasisFind minimum tissue tension — may combine direct action, exaggeration, disengagementPlace the region in neutral / idling firstPlace the region into the position of ease first
Force sourceThe patient's inherent physiologic motionPhysician adds a facilitating forcePhysician adds a facilitating force
Barrier relationNeither purely direct nor indirect — seeks balanceMostly indirectCombined indirect→direct
Timing~10 sec for a response; 20–30+ sec for release3–5 secNo hold
Exam cue phrases"stable bony platform," "fulcrum," "inherent forces," "balanced tension""neutral, compression, ease, 3–5 seconds""ease, compression/traction, move through neutral to barrier"

Fibula BLT — lateral recumbent, fibular head + lateral malleolus

OA BLT — posterior tubercle of C1 as the fulcrum

🧠 Memory Hook — the universal rib BLT idea

"Disengage → Stabilize → Rotate the vertebra AWAY → Breathe it home." Every rib BLT, seated or supine, is that sentence.

Q: A patient's clavicle is restricted and both the AC and SC joints feel stuck. Which arm does the patient place behind their back, and what is the sequence?

Answer

The contralateral arm goes behind the back — not the ipsilateral arm. She called this out specifically as a detail you'd have to know. Sequence: patient seated leans forward onto the physician's thumbs under the clavicle (disengagement), physician steers the shoulder posteriorly to engage AC tension and uses contralateral scapular retraction for the SC end, exaggerates toward ease, balances the clavicle in all four directions, applies direct action back toward neutral with an inhalation hold, then returns and rechecks SC/AC springing.

Q: A physician braces both sides of a joint, fine-tunes to minimum ligamentous tension, asks the patient to hold exhalation, and waits for softening. Which technique — and what is providing the corrective force?

Answer

BLT. The corrective force is the patient's own inherent physiologic forces — here, respiration. The physician supplies only the fulcrum and the balance, never a thrust or a resisted contraction.

Week 6 · LO 1–11
MFR was new; soft tissue was review

Dr. Yi ⭐ CONFIRMED ON THE EXAM

Myofascial Release & Soft Tissue

⚠ Settled in the session

There was an exchange between Dr. Stevens and Dr. Doan about whether MFR would be tested. Dr. Doan's answer: "it's on the list." It is being tested. She also stated at the start: "You have to know all of the treatment types that you've learned up to this point in time on the written exam, including the myofascial and soft tissue."

The compare-and-contrast slide from Dr. Yi's deck

Direct = into bind · Indirect = into ease

The core distinction

FeatureMyofascial Release (MFR)Soft Tissue (STT)
Direct / indirectDIRECT or INDIRECT — and you can move back and forth between themDIRECT only
Active / passiveACTIVE or PASSIVE — patient may help with breathing, eye movement, or gentle contractionPASSIVE only — the patient does nothing
Tissue targetThe fascia — the outer wrapping around muscle, and the fascial planes investing neurovascular structures, viscera, tendons, ligaments, periosteumThe musculature underneath the fascia — you go deeper than the fascia. Because you go deeper, it's direct
Depth of pressureOnly as deep as the layer you intend to engageMuch deeper pressure
FeedbackContinual palpatory feedback, following the tissue as it unwindsMonitors tone/pain/ROM, but not the same continuous unwinding feedback
Motion appliedStacked vectors in three dimensions; follow creep/release and change vectors as tissue changesLinear and longitudinal stretching, kneading, bowstringing, inhibition, traction
Hold20–30 sec, sometimes 60 — usually 30–60Rhythmic or sustained; no fixed count
Mechanism emphasisViscoelastic creep and hysteresis, fascial glide/hydration, mechanotransduction, proprioceptive and autonomic modulationReduced alpha motor neuron activity/spasm, improved circulation and lymphatic flow, stretch of shortened fascia, relaxation, improved ROM
🧠 Memory Hook — MFR vs Soft Tissue

"MFR wraps. Soft tissue digs." MFR engages the wrapping (fascia); soft tissue goes through it into the muscle — which is why soft tissue is always direct and passive and MFR can be anything.
"Soft tissue = 2 P's: Passive + Pressure (deep)."

Same end goal, shared indications

Both are used to remove restriction and restore homeostasis. Indicated when the patient has somatic dysfunction involving fascia, muscles, or related structures, to:

  • Relax hypertonic muscles
  • Decrease tone and density of fascial structures
  • Enhance circulation
  • Improve local and systemic immune response
  • Augment the autonomic nervous system
  • Provide a general state of relaxation

Fascia: definition, layers, functions (LO 5, 6, 8)

She paused specifically on this: "You need to know how to define fascia and differentiate it from connective tissue."

🧭 The three-term hierarchy

Connective tissue = the broad family of supporting tissues: fascia, blood, bone, fat, tendons, ligaments, and other extracellular-matrix-rich structures.
Fascia = a body-wide continuous connective-tissue network, mostly irregular collagenous fibers and ground substance, that invests, separates, suspends, protects, and connects muscles, organs, bones, nerves, vessels, tendons, ligaments, aponeuroses.
Myofascia = the portion of that network in direct relationship with skeletal muscle.

The four fascial layers

Core functions of fascia

LayerLocation / contentsClinical relevance
PannicularSuperficial/subcutaneous, beneath skin: collagen, elastin, fat, vessels, nervesUsually the first layer engaged in gentle MFR. Restrictions change skin drag, superficial glide, edema movement
Investing (axial/appendicular)Deep fascia of trunk and limbs; contributes to epimysium, periosteum, tendon sheathsThe major target for limb, axial, scapulothoracic, thoracolumbar, and plantar fascial techniques
MeningealDura and leptomeninges — coverings of the nervous systemLinks cranial, cervical, dural, sacral, and neurologic models. Treat gently and indirectly
VisceralOrgan fascial layers, mesenteries, broad ligament, root of lung; conduits for neurovascular bundlesRelevant to diaphragms, lymphatics, respiration, pelvic floor, visceral motion
🧠 Memory Hook — four layers, outside in

"Pants, Investments, Meninges, Viscera" → Pannicular (the skin's "pants") → Investing (deep, wraps muscle) → Meningeal (dura) → Visceral (organs). P-I-M-V, superficial to deep.

Functions of fascia — the list she read out

1

Protection & packing of viscera

Suspends, organizes, cushions organs and their conduits.

2

Transmission of fluids

Fascial planes carry lymphatics, veins, arteries, nerves, interstitial fluid across regions.

3

Structural support & locomotion

Reduces friction, assists gliding, connects muscle to bone, transmits force.

4

Proprioception & nociception

Richly innervated — position, movement, pressure, chemical, and pain information.

5

Mechanotransduction

Converts mechanical loading into cellular electrochemical signaling. Dose matters — the goal is useful input, not maximal force.

6

Metabolic & immune function

Macrophages, mast cells, fibroblasts, adipocytes, sympathetic input, hyaluronan viscosity.

7

Adaptation & postural control

Prolonged posture and repeated demand thicken, shorten, dehydrate, or bias fascial glide.

🧠 Memory Hook — fascial functions

"PT SPAM" → Protection/packing · Transmission of fluids · Structural support & locomotion · Proprioception/nociception · Adaptation/postural control · Mechanotransduction + Metabolic/immune.

Fascia through the five models

Fascia mapped onto the five pathophysiological models

ModelFascia connectionCase application
BiomechanicalSupports, stabilizes, balances, and transmits force across joints and regionsPlantar fascia restriction changes calf, hamstring, sacral, lumbar, and suboccipital tone through the posterior chain
Respiratory-circulatoryFascial planes house lymphatics and vessels; diaphragms pump fluidCongestion improves after thoracic inlet, respiratory diaphragm, and pelvic diaphragm work
NeurologicNeurovascular bundles are wrapped by fascia; fascia supplies proprioceptive and nociceptive inputCervical fascial restriction → altered neck proprioception, headache, pain sensitivity
Metabolic-energeticGlide, tension distribution, and efficient force transfer reduce the energy cost of posture and locomotionImproving thoracolumbar or LE glide makes standing/walking less metabolically expensive
BehavioralStress, guarding, breath holding, sleep posture, movement habits alter fascial tone and pain perceptionA stressed student with forward head posture and shallow breathing needs tissue work plus posture/breath coaching

MFR vocabulary you must be able to define

TermMeaningWhat your hands feel
EaseDirection of least resistance — used in indirect treatmentLess drag, softer end-feel, tissue follows easily
BindThe restrictive barrier — used in direct treatmentIncreased drag, tension, an early stop
CreepSlow deformation of tissue under sustained low loadThe barrier seems to melt or lengthen under steady contact
HysteresisEnergy lost as heat when tissue is loaded and unloadedWarmth, softening, a new resting position after release
TensegrityTensional integrity — continuous tension (fascia) with discontinuous compression elements (bone)Local force does not stay local; it distributes along connected lines

The MFR sequence

  1. Permission & positionComfortable position with broad, steady contact.
  2. Engage the intended layerSink only as far as needed: pannicular → superficial → investing/deep → periosteal.
  3. Motion test in multiple vectorsSuperior/inferior, medial/lateral, rotation, F/E, translation, compression/distraction, respiratory.
  4. Choose direct, indirect, or mixedDirect = into bind. Indirect = into ease. Mixed = some vectors each.
  5. Stack the barriersAdd one vector at a time until the contacted plane feels balanced or fully engaged.
  6. Add patient cooperationBreath, eye movement, gentle contraction, postural cooperation.
  7. Hold and follow the changeWait for temperature change, softening, creep, lengthening, reduced density. Re-stack as the tissue moves.
  8. Stop when release slows, then recheckCompare the exact tissue drag, ROM, tenderness, or respiratory motion you diagnosed.

Functional myofascial continuities (LO 9)

ContinuityWhat it linksClinical example
Superficial back linePlantar fascia → calf → hamstrings → sacrotuberous ligament → sacrum → erectors → suboccipitalsPlantar fascial restriction contributes to hamstring tension, sacral drag, suboccipital tone
Lateral lineLateral ankle/leg → IT band → lateral trunk → ribs → cervical sidebendersRecurrent ankle sprain or IT band tension relating to rib cage/cervical compensation
Functional front/back linesCross-body: shoulder girdle → trunk → pelvis → contralateral lower extremityLatissimus + thoracolumbar fascia transmit shoulder restriction into opposite gluteal/pelvic mechanics
Spiral lineOblique coiling/uncoiling through trunk and limbsRotational gait, scoliosis compensation, throwing mechanics
Neck-eye continuumCervical fascia, deep neck structures, ocular movementEye movements assist anterior/posterior cervical and suboccipital MFR
Diaphragm chainThoracic inlet → respiratory diaphragm → pelvic diaphragmTreating inlet + diaphragms improves respiratory excursion and fluid movement

Technique atlas — the ones shown in lab

She listed these by name: thoracic inlet/outlet (the top slide), abdominal MFR, popliteal MFR, interosseous membrane MFR, carpal tunnel MFR (Dr. Stevens covered this), plus arm and leg traction. For soft tissue: cervical, scapular, and lumbar soft tissue in class.

Superior thoracic aperture (thoracic inlet/outlet) MFR — treat this first

Soft tissue technique overview

TechniqueSetupRecipeHigh-yield cue
Superior thoracic aperture MFRSupine or seated. Finger pads on anterior first rib/costosternal; thumbs monitor first rib/costovertebral. Assess first rib, clavicle, clavipectoral fascia, inlet rotation/sidebending/F-EStack direct or indirect vectors until fascial tension engages or balances; use deep inhalation/hold or exhalation to assistTreat this region FIRST before any lymphatic/fluid-moving work
Suboccipital / posterior cervical MFRSupine, physician at head. Finger pads on suboccipital muscles below the inferior nuchal lineHold direct or indirect barrier 20–60 sec or until texture changes. Eye movement or breath helps (neck-eye continuum)Recheck OA/cervical motion and headache tenderness
Diaphragm domingSupine. Thumbs on costal cartilages a few inches lateral to xiphoid; fingers on rib shaftsAdvance thumbs cephalad under the ribs. On inhalation resist caudad motion; on exhalation take up slack cephaladCaution with significant CHF or acute respiratory distress
Pelvic diaphragm liftProne, clear consent and draping. Thumbs on medial surfaces of the ischial tuberositiesAllow descent during inhalation, take up slack cephalad during exhalation until the pelvic floor softens/liftsSame respiratory logic as the thoracic diaphragm

Sub-occipital release (STT)Supine, physician at head, finger pads below the inferior nuchal lineGentle direct sustained inhibition/traction into hypertonic tissue until it softensSame contact as suboccipital MFR — what makes it STT is direct sustained inhibition with a passive patient, not vector-stacked fascial work
⚠ Shared safety for both families

No consent or no cooperation is an absolute stop. Avoid or modify over unstable tissue, open wounds, acute fracture/dislocation, infection, major neurologic or vascular compromise, and suspected malignancy/metastasis.

Q: A technique uses continuous palpatory feedback, stacks fascial vectors in three dimensions, and can treat into either ease or bind while the patient assists with breathing. MFR or soft tissue?

Answer

MFR. Three tells, any one of which is decisive: vector stacking, the choice of ease or bind, and an active patient. Soft tissue is direct and passive only.

Q: Which fascial layer contains the dura and leptomeninges, and which model does it most connect to?

Answer

Meningeal fascia, most connected to the neurologic model — it links cranial, cervical, dural, and sacral relationships. Treat gently and indirectly.

Week 1 · Week 8
"High yield, Down syndrome"

Choosing, sequencing, and stopping

Technique Selection, Sequencing & Contraindications

Her slide from her own board review, "because it comes up a lot." You don't need it in enormous detail yet — but the sequencing rules and the contraindication lists are straightforwardly testable.

Choosing the technique

FactorRule
Age / frailtyOlder patients generally do better with indirect techniques — unless the patient is very sick, when a direct technique may be needed to make them better
CognitionMental health and cognition drive whether the patient can participate at all
Frequency — acute vs chronicMore frequent treatment if acute; less frequent if chronic
Frequency — ageMore frequent with children (they bounce back faster); less frequent with older adults
Number of areas treatedTreat fewer areas if the patient is unhealthy or sick
Risk / benefitAlways weighed against the patient's reserve — this is the metabolic-energetic model applied to your own treatment plan

Sequencing — the order of operations

  1. Thoracic inlet / outlet FIRST"You treat that area first so that you can open up the drainage system." If you're treating the head, things can drain down; if the body, things can drain up. Usually treated with BLT or MFR. (UNE says "outlet"; she says "inlet" — same region.)
  2. Thoracic spine BEFORE ribsA rib that feels posterior may just be following a rotated thoracic vertebra through the costotransverse ligament. Treat the thoracic problem and the "posterior rib" often disappears.
  3. Then lumbar or cervicalDepends on the person and what they came in for.
  4. Axial skeleton BEFORE extremitiesUnless there's a muscle spasm in the extremity — then treat the spasm first. It all depends on what they came to see you for.
🧠 Memory Hook — sequencing

"Open the door before you clean the house." Inlet/outlet opens the drainage door. Then: "Spine before ribs, core before limbs — unless something is screaming."

Technique-specific "do not use" rules

⚠ The three she said out loud
  • Do NOT use muscle energy if the patient cannot understand directions — young children, cognitive delay, dementia. ME requires an active, cooperative patient.
  • Do NOT use HVLA, articulatory, or any direct technique in bony areas with growth or compromise based on injury or age, or where there is osteoporosis at that joint.
  • Children with Down syndrome: NO direct techniques. She flagged this twice — "High yield, Down syndrome. Don't do that." (The reason is atlantoaxial instability.)

Contraindications to OMM overall

🛑

ABSOLUTE contraindications

  • Lack of consent
  • Unable to participate in treatment or follow directions — including patients who cannot stay passive/in place because they move around too much
  • Treatment over an open wound or sutured area
  • Instability of the bony architecture
⚖️

RELATIVE contraindications

"You might be able to do a bit, depends on what kind of treatment you're doing."

  • Dislocation
  • Fractures
  • Neurologic compromise
  • Vascular compromise
  • Malignancy / metastasis
  • Infection
  • Bleeding
🧠 Memory Hook — absolute vs relative

Absolute = the 4 things that make treatment impossible or reckless no matter the technique: "No consent, no participation, no skin, no stability."
Relative = the pathology list: "D-F-N-V-M-I-B" — Dislocation, Fracture, Neurologic, Vascular, Malignancy, Infection, Bleeding. Every one of those is "depends on which technique," not "never."

🔑 The recheck rule

Whether written or practical: the treatment isn't finished until you recheck. The treatment rubric gives explicit weight to recheck and efficacy — tissue texture change, ROM improvement, and pain reduction matter more than performing memorized choreography.

Q: A 7-year-old with Down syndrome has a cervical somatic dysfunction. Which technique category is contraindicated, and why?

Answer

All direct techniques — HVLA and articulatory especially. The concern is atlantoaxial instability, common in Down syndrome. She flagged this twice as high-yield. Choose indirect: counterstrain, FPR, BLT, or gentle MFR.

Q: A patient presents for treatment of a lumbar dysfunction, and also has a congested-sounding chest and lower-extremity edema. In what order do you treat, and why?

Answer

Thoracic inlet/outlet first — usually with BLT or MFR — to open the drainage system, so that fluid mobilized from below has somewhere to go. Then thoracic spine, then ribs, then lumbar. Treating the periphery before opening the inlet just moves fluid into a closed system.

Spinal root vs peripheral nerve — the differentiation LO

Exam clueSpinal nerve rootPeripheral nerve
Pain originNeck/back pain with limb radiationLocal tunnel/entrapment pain; may not involve the spine at all
Sensory patternDermatomal (borders may be fuzzy — dermatomes overlap)Named nerve distribution; sharper demarcation
Weakness patternMyotomal — muscles sharing a root are weak even if supplied by different peripheral nervesOnly muscles supplied by that one peripheral nerve; same-root muscles from other nerves are spared
ReflexesRoot-level reflex asymmetryUsually preserved unless that nerve carries the reflex arc
ProvocationSpurling, shoulder abduction relief, SLR, slump, femoral stretch, cough/ValsalvaTinel, Phalen, cubital tunnel compression, fibular head compression
PalpationUsually not reproducible by pressing superficial tissue over the painful areaMay reproduce at the entrapment site or trigger point

Radiculitis vs radiculopathy vs myelopathy

TermPrimary problemTypical findingsAction
RadiculitisInflamed/irritated nerve rootRadiating pain and paresthesia; no clear objective weakness or reflex lossConservative care; monitor for progression
RadiculopathyRoot dysfunction from compression/inflammation/ischemia — conduction blockDermatomal sensory change, myotomal weakness, and/or reflex lossLocalize the root; image/EMG if severe, unclear, progressive, or persistent
MyelopathySpinal cord dysfunctionUMN signs: gait instability, hand clumsiness, spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, Hoffman, Babinski, possible bowel/bladderRED FLAG. Urgent imaging/referral — not a segmental problem
Peripheral neuropathyDisease of peripheral nervesNamed nerve or stocking-glove patternDon't call stocking-glove loss a single root lesion
🧠 Memory Hook — the -itis / -opathy / -myelo ladder

"-itis = Irritated (pain only). -opathy = Objective deficit. Myelo = Motor neuron UP (UMN)." Pain alone climbs no further than radiculitis; a deficit makes it radiculopathy; a UMN sign moves it to the cord.

The differential map — "compare and contrast"

These are the words she said you'll see as compare-and-contrast items: spondylolisthesis, spondylolysis, spondylosis — "they're all different."

Pars fracture (Scotty dog) and vertebral slippage

Palpable step-off suggests spondylolisthesis

🧠 Memory Hook — the spondylo family

"-LYSIS = Loss of the pars" (a fracture — the Scotty dog collar).
"-LISTHESIS = Lets go and slides" (thesis = to slip; anterior displacement of one vertebra on another).
"-OSIS = Old" (degenerative DJD change — she literally said "Osis is old").
"-ARTHROPATHY = Autoimmune" (inflammatory, HLA-B27, not wear and tear).

ConditionPathophysiologyVignette clueImage clue
Spinal stenosisNarrowing of the canal/lateral recess/foramen from DJD, osteophytes, disc bulge, ligamentum flavum, facet hypertrophyLow back and leg pain. Worse upright / in extension. BETTER leaning forward — "leaning on a grocery cart makes them feel better than standing straight up." Neurogenic claudicationCentral canal narrowing on MRI/CT
Disc herniationNucleus pulposus through the annulus. The posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow, so herniation goes posterolateralOpposite of stenosis: worse leaning forward / with flexion, sitting, cough, sneeze. Pain, numbness down the leg. SpondylolisthesisAnterior displacement (slippage) of one vertebra relative to another. May follow a pars defect (isthmic) or be degenerativeMechanical low back pain, hamstring tightness; radicular symptoms if the foramen narrows. Palpable step-offLateral x-ray shows the slip. L5–S1 classic for isthmic; L4–L5 for degenerative

🧠 Memory Hook — stenosis vs disc

"CART = CANAL." If leaning on the shopping cart helps, it's stenosis — flexion opens the canal. If bending forward hurts, it's the disc. They are exact opposites, and the exam loves that pair.

Central canal stenosis

Neurogenic claudication — relief with flexion or sitting

Psoas syndrome — memorize the full finding set

🩺 The six findings she listed
  • Spasm of the psoas / iliopsoas — behaves like a flexion contracture
  • Positive Thomas test
  • Tender point medial to the ASIS
  • Non-neutral L1–L2 dysfunction to the SAME side
  • Pelvic side shift to the CONTRALATERAL side
  • Sacral dysfunction on an oblique axis
  • Contralateral piriformis spasm
🧠 Memory Hook — psoas syndrome sidedness

"SAME spine, OPPOSITE everything else." The L1–L2 dysfunction is on the same side as the tight psoas; the pelvic side shift and the piriformis spasm are contralateral. That sidedness split is the whole question.

Piriformis syndrome — sciatic nerve under/through the piriformis

"You should be able to identify one of these patterns if you see a picture like this — know whether it's an L3, L4, L5, or S1 pattern." She noted the same slide is in Dr. Bissette's lower-extremity deck too.

"L4 = the floor (heel walk, patellar). L5 = the big toe. S1 = the small toe (and Achilles)." Or the walking test: L4–L5 can't heel-walk; S1 can't toe-walk.

🧠 Memory Hook — cauda equina

"S-B-B: Saddle, Bowel/Bladder, Bilateral." Any one of the three in a back-pain patient = stop, do not treat, send them in. She called it "potty plunger" territory: saddle anesthesia + loss of bowel or bladder control.

Lhermitte, Hoffman, Spurling, SLR, Kemp's

Step-off, percussion, clonus, Babinski

TestHow to performPositive findingMeaning
Spurling's maneuverTurn the head TOWARD the symptomatic side, extend and sidebend, then apply gentle axial compression. Check both sides. If pain is severe, minimal rotation/sidebending is enoughIpsilateral arm radicular pain/paresthesiaSpecific confirmatory test for cervical radiculopathy
Lhermitte's signFlex the neckElectric shock down the spine or into the limbsCentral cord / dorsal column irritation: myelopathy, MS, tumor, B12, whiplash

Crossed SLRRaise the asymptomatic legPain reproduced in the symptomatic legMore specific for disc herniation

Babinski signStroke the lateral plantar foot heel→forefoot, then mediallyGreat toe dorsiflexion / fanningUMN sign

🧠 Memory Hook — which tests are CORD tests?

"L-H-C-B" — Lhermitte, Hoffman, Clonus, Babinski. Those four (plus gait change and fine-motor decline) convert a "neck pain" question into a myelopathy workup question. Spurling and SLR are root tests; they never make the answer "MRI now."

OMT safety in radicular patients (LO 12–13)

SituationOMT indicated?Reasoning
Somatic dysfunction + mild stable radicular symptoms, normal neuro examOften yes, with cautionGentle indirect/soft tissue/traction-style care can reduce nociception and improve mechanics
Acute severe radicular pain, no progressive deficitSelective and gentleUse pain-free positions; do not compress into symptoms
Progressive weakness, bowel/bladder symptoms, saddle anesthesiaNo routine OMT firstEmergency workup/referral is the priority
Myelopathy signs (hyperreflexia, clonus, Babinski, gait disturbance)Contraindication to aggressive OMTPossible cord compression — imaging and specialty management
Fracture, malignancy, infection, severe osteoporosis, instabilityContraindicated or heavily modifiedRisk exceeds benefit until clarified
Prior spine surgery/fusion/hardwareRequires history + imaging contextGentle non-thrust techniques around, not through, vulnerable segments
🔑 The peripheralization rule

During any treatment of a radicular patient: if leg or arm symptoms move farther down the limb, stop or modify. Peripheralization means the position or force is wrong. Prefer positions that centralize symptoms.

Q: A 68-year-old can walk only two blocks before her legs ache and she must sit. She reports that leaning on a shopping cart lets her walk much farther. What is the diagnosis, and what is the mechanism of the relief?

Answer

Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication. Leaning forward flexes the lumbar spine, which opens the central canal and the neuroforamina; standing upright and extending narrows them. This is the exact mirror image of a disc herniation, where flexion worsens symptoms.

Q: A 40-year-old has neck pain radiating to the middle finger, a diminished triceps reflex, and Spurling's reproduces the arm symptoms. Which root, and what is the single most likely underlying cause if he were 65 instead of 40?

Answer

C7 — the most common cervical root (~70%), classically mapping to the triceps reflex and the middle finger. At 40, think disc herniation. At 65, think spondylosis — degenerative DJD with foraminal narrowing is the most common cause of cervical root compression symptoms in older patients ("osis is old").

Q: A patient with low back pain and left buttock pain has normal reflexes and strength, and exquisite tenderness over the greater trochanter. Radiculopathy or something else?

Answer

Trochanteric bursitis / greater trochanteric pain syndrome. The focal palpation finding plus a normal neuro exam dominates. Bursitis may radiate but usually not past the knee, and never with a dermatomal sensory loss or reflex change.

Lower Extremity

🔑 First, the four buckets

Every lower-extremity complaint sorts into one of four etiologies before you do anything else — she said Dr. Bissette wants you to know the difference between spinal nerve, peripheral nerve, myofascial, and articular causes.

BucketPain patternExam cluesClassic examples
Spinal nerve / radicularDermatomal; may radiate below the kneeMyotomal weakness, altered reflex, sensory deficit, positive SLR or femoral stretch; lumbar motion reproduces symptomsL4–S3 irritation causing sciatica; an L5 pattern can mimic foot drop
Peripheral nerveNamed nerve territory, not a dermatomeTinel/compression at the entrapment site; weakness only in that nerve's muscles; reflexes sparedCommon fibular nerve at the fibular head → foot drop; lateral femoral cutaneous → meralgia paresthetica; interdigital nerve → Morton neuroma
MyofascialRegional aching/referral that ignores dermatomesTART changes; the trigger point reproduces the familiar pain; normal neuro screenPiriformis referral, hamstring tender points, IT band friction, plantar fascial tension
ArticularDeep joint-line pain, groin pain for hip, mechanical catching/locking, weight-bearing painRestricted ROM or painful end-feel, crepitus, effusion, instability, positive joint-specific testsHip/knee OA, labral tear, meniscal tear, ligament sprain, SI joint dysfunction

Gait phases & the arches

She listed the phases directly: heel strike → foot flat → heel off/heel up → pre-swing (toe-off).

Gait phases

The foot as a tripod — heel, 1st MT head, 4th/5th MT heads

Gait momentWhat's happeningKey muscle / fascial ideaWhat dysfunction looks like
Heel strikeInitial contact through the heelTibialis anterior contracts eccentrically so the foot doesn't slapFoot drop → toe drag, tripping, foot-flat contact instead of heel strike
Foot flatLoading response; the arch lowers to absorb shockPlantar fascia + intrinsics control pronation and arch descentPes planus, dropped navicular/cuboid → overloads plantar fascia, knee, hip, pelvis
Heel offTerminal stance; heel rises as the body moves over the forefootGastroc-soleus contracts concentrically and tightens the arch for propulsionWeak push-off, Achilles/gastroc restriction, forefoot pain, shortened stride
Pre-swingToe-off before swingToe flexors + the windlass effect convert the foot from flexible platform to rigid leverHallux valgus, Morton neuroma, transverse arch collapse, first-ray restriction
ArchBonesDysfunction implication
Medial longitudinalCalcaneus, talus, navicular, cuneiforms, first three raysCollapse → pes planus, plantar fascial strain, tibial internal rotation, genu valgum, pelvic and lumbar/SI compensation
Lateral longitudinalCalcaneus, cuboid, fourth/fifth raysCuboid dysfunction or lateral overload → ankle instability, knee varus loading
TransverseMaintains metatarsal-head spacingFlattening → calluses and irritation of the interdigital neurovascular bundle — especially between toes 3 and 4 (Morton neuroma)

Fibula & tibia mechanics — the coupling she walked through

🧭 The rules
  • The proximal and distal fibula move in opposite directions: if the proximal fibula goes anterior, the distal fibula goes posterior, and vice versa.
  • The proximal fibular head glides ANTERIOR with PRONATION of the foot — the sole rolls outward/laterally (eversion, dorsiflexion, abduction).
  • The proximal fibular head glides POSTERIOR with SUPINATION — the sole rolls inward/medially (plantarflexion, inversion, adduction).
  • The tibia externally rotates with knee extension and does a posterolateral glide (the screw-home mechanism).
🧠 Memory Hook — fibular head

"PA / SP" — Pronation → fibular head Anterior. Supination → fibular head Posterior. The alphabet even helps: P before S, A before P.
And: "Proximal and distal are always opposite."

Ottawa rules — memorize both lists

Ottawa ankle rules — the red zones are the bony tenderness points

Ottawa knee rules

🦶

Ottawa ANKLE / FOOT — get an x-ray if…

  • Bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of the LATERAL malleolus (distal 6 cm)
  • Bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of the MEDIAL malleolus
  • Bone tenderness at the NAVICULAR
  • Bone tenderness at the BASE OF THE FIFTH METATARSAL
  • Inability to bear weight for 4 steps both immediately after injury and in the emergency department / at evaluation

Subjective pain in the malleolar or midfoot zone is the gate — but it's bony tenderness that triggers the film, not vague swelling.

🦵

Ottawa KNEE — get an x-ray if…

  • Age ≥ 55
  • Isolated tenderness of the patella
  • Tenderness at the head of the fibula
  • Inability to flex the knee to 90°
  • Inability to bear weight for 4 steps immediately and at evaluation
🧠 Memory Hook — Ottawa

Ankle: "2 Malleoli, 1 Navicular, 1 Fifth, 4 Steps."
Knee: "55 · Patella · Fibular head · 90 · 4 steps." — she pointed out that fibular head tenderness is the one people forget.

Ankle sprain grading

Grading of ankle sprains

Mechanism: the ligament or capsule is stretched beyond its elastic limit, rupturing some fibers. Most common site is the LATERAL ankle, because people roll the foot in (inversion) and the ATFL and calcaneofibular ligament are weaker than the deltoid ligament medially. Deltoid sprains are uncommon — think a basketball player landing awkwardly.

GradeInjuryFindingsManagement
Grade IStretch or slight tearNo functional loss, no instability; mild–moderate swellingProtection, relative rest, early ROM, rehab, gentle OMT if safe
Grade IIIncomplete tear, classically the ATFLTenderness on ATFL palpation, pain with walking, mild instability, severe swelling over a >4 cm areaBrace/immobilize as needed, rehab, reassess stability; image if Ottawa positive
Grade IIIComplete tear, often ATFL + CFLUnable to bear weight at all, mechanical instability/disability, major swellingRefer / image. Do not try to "fix" instability with aggressive OMT

Collateral ligament grading & the terrible triad

InjuryMechanismGradingTreatment direction
MCLValgus stress (sports/skiing)I: stretched, no laxity · II: 5–10 mm laxity with a firm endpoint · III: complete tear, no firm endpoint, laxity in extensionI–II conservative; III → surgical consult, especially with ACL/meniscus injury
LCLVarus stress; evaluate the posterolateral cornerI: no laxity · II: 5–10 mm with endpoint · III: complete tear, often with PLC/cruciate injuryI–II conservative; III commonly surgical repair. MRI is the gold standard for grading

Ligamentous injury and the O'Donoghue "terrible triad"

🔑 O'Donoghue's triad / terrible triad / unhappy triad

Classically: ACL tear + MCL tear + MEDIAL MENISCUS tear. Mechanism is a lateral blow to a planted knee → rapid swelling, instability, medial joint-line pain, possible locking.

Note: the auto-transcript of the review session renders this as "MCL, LCL, and the ACL," which is almost certainly a transcription slip for "MCL, medial meniscus, and the ACL." Go with ACL + MCL + medial meniscus — that's what the Week 5 course notes and every standard source say. Some newer descriptions note lateral meniscus involvement in variants.

🧠 Memory Hook — terrible triad

"A-M-M" — ACL, MCL, Medial meniscus. All three live on or cross the medial side of a knee that got hit from the lateral side.

Common foot & ankle conditions

Pes cavus vs pes planus

Morton neuroma — classically between toes 3 and 4

ConditionPresentationDriverTreatment / OMM angle
Pes cavusHigh, rigid arch; lateral loading; pain despite an arch that "looks present"Reduced shock absorption; can be structural or neurologicScreen neuro if new or asymmetric; footwear/orthotics; treat ankle, fibula, pelvis, spine compensations
Pes planusFlat medial arch, weight-bearing on the navicular, pronationMedial arch collapse; drives tibial internal rotation and genu valgumArch support; treat navicular/cuboid/cuneiform, talocrural restriction, upstream pelvic/axial compensation
Plantar fasciitisHeel/plantar pain, worst with the first steps in the morning; possible heel spurRepetitive microtrauma → increased plantar fascial tension. Risks: flat arch, weight, pregnancy, poor shoesOMT to arch/foot/ankle/calf, stretching, supportive shoes/orthotics, NSAIDs
Hallux valgus / bunionPainful red great toe; proximal lateral deviation, distal medial deviation; toes may crossAltered forefoot loading, tight/high-heel shoes, family history, RA. More common in womenWider toe box, toe spacers, arch support, OMT for first ray, NSAIDs; surgery if refractory

Foot dropCatching toes, tripping, weak dorsiflexion, dorsal foot/lateral leg sensory symptomsCommon fibular nerve at the fibular head, cast/bedrail compression, trauma, L5 radiculopathy, or central causesNeuro exam + referral if progressive/traumatic; AFO for safety; treat fibular head/peroneal tunnel and lumbar/pelvic contributors
🧠 Memory Hook — Morton & foot drop

"Morton lives at 3-4 and hates tight shoes." Transverse arch collapse squeezes the nerve between the 3rd and 4th metatarsal heads.
"Foot drop = fibular head OR L5." Two answers, always. Peripheral = fibular nerve at the fibular head; root = L5. Motor weakness earns a real neuro exam.

"vaLgus = knees say heLLo (L for 'together'). Varus = bow-legged, like a VARiety of space between." Or: valgus — the distal segment points away from midline, so the knee falls in.

Hip pain by region

LocationLikely diagnosesPresentation / examImaging
Anterior / groinHip OA, labral tear, FAI, flexor/adductor strain, meralgia paresthetica if the symptom is anterolateral sensoryHip OA: older, gradual, antalgic gait, limited flexion and internal rotation.
