🩺 Meralgia paresthetica — the board-style discriminator

Sensory-only pain/dysesthesia of the anterolateral thigh from lateral femoral cutaneous nerve compression at the inguinal ligament. Normal strength, normal reflexes. Risks: obesity, pregnancy, tight belts / tool belts, diabetes, alcohol, lead.
If hip flexion, adduction, or quadriceps strength is weak — it is NOT meralgia. Think beyond it.

Sciatica & its differential

Sciatica pain distributions

🔑 Definition

Pain extending from the low back or buttock, down the posterolateral thigh, to the foot, from irritation of the sciatic nerve or its contributing roots L4–S3. "Sciatica" is a pain distribution, not a diagnosis — your job is to name the generator.

DifferentialSupports it
Lumbar radiculopathyDermatomal pain/paresthesia, myotomal weakness, reflex change, positive SLR/slump; symptoms change with lumbar motion
Piriformis syndromeGradual buttock pain worse with sitting; palpation of the piriformis reproduces it; normal lumbar neuro screen
SI joint dysfunctionButtock/posterior pelvic pain; may follow pregnancy, leg-length discrepancy, scoliosis, OA, spondyloarthropathy. Use a cluster of provocation tests: FABER, Gaenslen, distraction, thigh thrust, lateral compression, sacral thrust
Myofascial referralTrigger point reproduces the familiar pain; non-dermatomal map; normal neuro exam
Peripheral/cutaneous nerveNamed-nerve territory: lateral femoral cutaneous, common fibular, tarsal tunnel, interdigital
🧭 Piriformis syndrome — the six described manifestations

Trauma to the gluteal region · pain on piriformis palpation · pain with stooping/lifting sometimes relieved by traction · palpable sausage-shaped piriformis mass · positive Lasègue sign · mild gluteal atrophy.

Lower-extremity screening exam sequence

  1. Observe before touchingGait, stairs, transitions, ADLs, shoe type and shoe wear pattern, whether they favor a leg.
  2. Standing inspectionArch height, gastroc/Achilles line, patellar position, genu varum/valgum, weight-bearing symmetry, edema, posture, leg-length clues.
  3. Supine inspectionPlantar skin, calluses, warts, coloration, hair growth, pulses, edema, apparent leg length.
  4. Hip ROM & strengthFlexion, extension, IR/ER, ab/adduction bilaterally. Stabilize the pelvis for extension so the patient can't roll into false motion.
  5. KneeFlex/ext, tibial IR/ER, screw-home, varus/valgus glide, A/P tibial glide, patellar motion, effusion/mechanical signs.
  6. Fibular headCompare anterolateral vs posteromedial glide. Relate to ankle sprain, fibular nerve symptoms, IT band/peroneal tension.
  7. Ankle & footTalocrural dorsi/plantarflexion at the talus, subtalar inversion/eversion through the calcaneus, forefoot, toes, navicular, cuboid, cuneiforms, metatarsals.
  8. Name, treat, recheckState the region, direction of ease/restriction, likely pain generator, and pre/post effect.

Lab technique recipes

TechniqueSetupCore steps
BLT tibia — seated kneeSeated; screen tibial IR/ER, varus/valgus, A/P glideKnee between physician's knees; compress tibia toward femur; fingers monitor MCL/LCL and tibial plateau; fine-tune rotation, varus/valgus, A/P glide into balanced tension; hold until warmth/softening/release
BLT knee — supineWhen the patient can't sit; physician seated at the sideTrap the ankle between arm/thorax; grasp proximal tibia/fibula; body lean for compression/distraction; motion-test A/P and varus/valgus; patient rotates the femur medially/laterally for postural cooperation
BLT patellaAssess superior/inferior, medial/lateral, and clockwise/counterclockwise patellar motionLift the patella anteriorly to disengage it from the femur, then use it as a handle on the knee capsule; stack directions; add dorsi/plantarflexion or knee flex/ext
BLT talocrural — "boot jack"Supine, physician at the footGrasp calcaneus and neck of talus between thenar eminences; thumbs at malleoli; inferior traction to disengage the talus; balance inversion/eversion, F/E, medial/lateral rotation; patient plantarflexes against resistance, then flexes knee/hip 1–2 inches while traction is maintained. Relax the knee first, then the foot
Still — midfootSupine; navicular, cuboid, cuneiformsThumbs/thenar on dorsum, fingers plantar; place midfoot bones into collective ease; add compression toward the restricted joint; carry through the arc toward the barrier; repeat 2–3×
BLT hip / femoroacetabularSeated figure-4, restricted hip crossed over the opposite kneePhysician stabilizes the medial crossed femur near the hip joint; patient holds the crossed knee and slowly circles the trunk/hip; pause or repeat in restricted arcs. Lecture cue: "the femur/physician is the bolt; the patient is the nut."
HVLA tibial rotationDiagnose externally or internally rotated tibia relative to the patellaExternally rotated tibia: internally rotate tibia, flex knee to barrier, short J-motion thrust medial→lateral. Internally rotated: externally rotate, flex to barrier, thrust lateral→medial. Avoid with acute instability, fracture, severe sprain, or no consent
Counterstrain — lateral hamstringBiceps femoris tender point just below the ischial tuberosity, or ~1/3 above the distal fibular-head attachmentProne; markedly flex the knee, externally rotate the tibia on the femur, fine-tune hip extension/compression until tenderness drops; hold 90 sec
Counterstrain — medial hamstringSemimembranosus/semitendinosus tender pointProne; markedly flex the knee, internally rotate the tibia on the femur, fine-tune; hold 90 sec
🧠 Memory Hook — hamstring counterstrain

"Point to the side you rotate toward." Lateral hamstring tender point → external rotation of the tibia. Medial → internal rotation. Both start with marked knee flexion.

Q: A patient rolls their ankle, has lateral swelling, cannot take four steps, and has bone tenderness at the posterior edge of the lateral malleolus. What is your next step, before any OMT?

Answer

X-ray — the Ottawa ankle rules are positive on two counts (posterior malleolar bone tenderness AND inability to bear weight for 4 steps). Only after fracture is excluded do you grade the sprain and consider OMT. A Grade III with instability gets referred regardless.

Q: A patient's foot pronates. Which direction has the proximal fibular head most likely glided, and which way has the distal fibula gone?

Answer

Proximal fibular head glides ANTERIOR with pronation (sole rolls outward/laterally: eversion, dorsiflexion, abduction). Because the proximal and distal fibula always move in opposite directions, the distal fibula goes POSTERIOR.

Week 7 · LO 1–11
Dr. Stevens

Nerve vs joint vs tendon vs myofascial

Upper Extremity

Same opening structure as the lower extremity: sort the complaint into spinal nerve, peripheral nerve, articular/tendon, or myofascial before you name a diagnosis. Then know the history/physical signs of the neurovascular entrapments and the diagnostic tests.

Differentiating peripheral entrapment from C8 radiculopathy

Myofascial referred pain — "the whole thing can act like it's something else"

🧭 The myofascial mimic slide she spent time on

She walked through referral maps for serratus posterior superior, serratus anterior, pectoralis major and others — "look at all the different places serratus posterior superior can have myofascial referred pain, just from that area." The point: a trigger point can produce arm and hand pain that looks radicular. You differentiate it with Spurling's and the neuro exam — myofascial referral has no myotomal weakness and no reflex change, and palpating the trigger point reproduces the familiar symptom.

Nerve entrapment map

EntrapmentNerve / locationSigns & symptomsKey discriminator
Thoracic Outlet SyndromeBrachial plexus and subclavian artery/vein compressed near the scalenes, first rib/clavicle, or pec minorNeurogenic: arm paresthesia, heaviness, weakness with overhead posture. Vascular: swelling, coolness, color change, pulse changesAdson's test — know how to perform it correctly. OMM targets first rib, clavicle, thoracic inlet, scalenes, pec minor — only after serious vascular compromise is excluded

EMG/NCS is the GOLD STANDARD — she emphasized this twice

🧠 Memory Hook — the ulnar pair, and the digit map

"CUBital = eLBow. GUYon = wrist (the guy at the wrist gate)." Both give you digits 4–5 — only the Tinel location separates them, and C8 radiculopathy mimics both.
Digit map: "Median = Middle three + thumb. Ulnar = Under (4½ + 5). Radial = Rear (dorsum/web space)." Median covers thumb, index, middle, and the radial half of the ring; ulnar takes the ulnar half of the ring plus the little finger.

Shoulder

Rotator cuff and impingement special tests

Adhesive capsulitis — exam and treatment

ConditionPresentationExam & testsManagement / OMT
Rotator cuff impingement / tearCompression of the SITS tendons and bursa under the coracoacromial arch; painful arc 60–120°; supraspinatus most commonly involvedNeer and Hawkins-Kennedy = impingement. Empty can = supraspinatus. Lift-off = subscapularis. Drop-arm = supraspinatus (full tear). Differentiate from C4/C5 radiculopathy with SpurlingX-ray first for bony/calcific disease; MRI for suspected tear. Rest/ice/activity modification/PT 6–8 weeks. OMT to rib, clavicle, scapula, GH mechanics
Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder)Progressive restriction of BOTH active and passive GH ROM. Risks: diabetes, thyroid disease, immobilization, female sex, Parkinson, stroke, impingementCapsular pattern: external rotation most limited, then abduction, then flexion. Scapular substitution is the major clue — the scapula takes over to move the arm. Negative biceps, drop-arm, crepitus, painful arcOften 1–3 years, but PT/OMM hastens recovery. Seven stages of Spencer is high-yield. Steroid injection may help early pain
Biceps tendonitisAnterior shoulder ache from the proximal biceps tendon, from overuse / wear and tear; often coexists with rotator cuff tear or SLAP lesionBicipital groove tenderness; positive Speed's and Yergason's tests. Popping/catching/locking suggests SLAPRest, PT, activity modification, NSAIDs, selective steroid injection; surgical referral for labral/cuff tear
Labral tear / SLAPThrowing athletes; painful shoulder with clicking/popping/clunkClunk test; MR arthrogram is the imaging of choice (contrast added to see it better)Conservative trial if mild; sports med/ortho if persistent mechanical symptoms

Avoid aggressive OMT across an unstable separation

🧠 Memory Hook — adhesive capsulitis

"E-A-F: External rotation goes first, then Abduction, then Flexion." That's the capsular pattern.
And the discriminator she stressed: "Everything hurts, in every direction, and the SCAPULA takes over." Frozen shoulder gives you a negative biceps test, negative drop-arm, no crepitus, no painful arc — just global restriction with scapular substitution. That absence pattern is the answer.

🧠 Memory Hook — rotator cuff tests

"Empty the can, Drop the arm → Supraspinatus. Lift off → Subscapularis. Neer & Hawkins → impingement."
SITS = Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor, Subscapularis. Painful arc 60–120°.

Elbow & forearm

Medial and lateral epicondylitis

Nursemaid's elbow — radial head subluxation

🎾

Lateral epicondylitis — TENNIS elbow

  • Overuse of the forearm EXTENSORS and SUPINATORS
  • Pain over the lateral epicondyle
  • Worse with wrist EXTENSION (resisted)
  • Racket sports; dominant arm common
  • Differentiate from radial tunnel/PIN and cervical radiculopathy
  • Treat: NSAIDs, rest, ice, elbow (counterforce) strap, OMT — counterstrain and MFR
⛳

Medial epicondylitis — GOLFER'S / little league elbow

  • Overuse of the forearm FLEXORS and PRONATORS
  • Pain over the medial epicondyle, may radiate down the anterior forearm
  • Worse with wrist FLEXION (resisted) and pronation
  • Rule out ligament instability, fracture, synovitis, radiculopathy
  • Treat: rest, ice, elbow strap, cock-up wrist splint if severe, NSAIDs, PT, OMT — counterstrain and MFR
🧠 Memory Hook — epicondylitis

"LET / MF" — Lateral = Extensors = Tennis. Medial = Flexors (+ pronators) = golf.
And she said this twice: "Make sure you know how to do counterstrain for medial and lateral epicondylitis" — it was in lab as a review.
Anatomical position check: "Lateral is the thumb side when the palm faces forward."

ConditionPresentationEvaluationTreatment
Radial head dysfunctionAnterior radial head ↔ restricted pronation. Posterior radial head ↔ restricted supinationPalpate radial head glide during pronation/supination; decide articular vs soft-tissue barrierRadial head ME, BLT/MFR/articulatory; recheck pronation/supination
Nursemaid's elbowRadial head subluxation from the annular ligament, children 12–35 months, after axial traction on the arm. Arm held flexed and pronated, reluctant to moveAssess fracture risk, vasculolymphatic integrity, elbow stability; image if atypical traumaSupination-flexion reduction. Refer for >1 week duration, recurrence, or failed reduction
Olecranon bursitisPosterior elbow swelling from trauma/overuse, gout/pseudogout/psoriatic arthritis, or infectionTwo-thirds are non-septic. Erythema suggests infection but fever may be absent. Aspiration is the gold standard when septic/crystal is a concernNon-infectious: rest, ice, NSAIDs, compression. Septic: antibiotics. Never OMT over an infected bursa
🔑 The FOOSH → radial head question

Her exact framing: "If somebody falls forward on an outstretched hand, their arms are in a PRONATED position, and therefore you will probably have a POSTERIOR radial head." If someone falls backward, you'll probably get a supination problem in the radial head. She said licensing questions ask it exactly that way.

Then match the treatment: for an anterior radial head (restricted pronation), take the forearm into pronation to the barrier and have the patient supinate against resistance for 3–5 sec. For a posterior radial head (restricted supination), take it into supination to the barrier and have the patient pronate against resistance.

🧠 Memory Hook — radial head ME

"Push them the way they can't go; make them fight back the way they want to." ME is direct — you engage the restricted direction and the patient contracts toward ease. So anterior head → you pronate, they supinate. Posterior head → you supinate, they pronate.
And: "Fall Forward = Pronated = Posterior."

Wrist & hand

Carpal tunnel exam and EMG — EMG/NCS is the gold standard

Gamekeeper's / skier's thumb — UCL of the first MCP

🧠 Memory Hook — the finger injury pair

"JERSEY = can't FLEX (you grabbed the jersey and the FDP tore off). MALLET = can't EXTEND (a mallet hit the tip and the extensor tore off)."
And the treatment split: "Jersey → surgeon. Mallet → splint in extension × 6 weeks."

🧠 Memory Hook — hand trauma workflow

"X-ray BEFORE you stress it." Gamekeeper's thumb: film first, then stress test. Boxer's fracture: film, then check rotation — nails should line up and every fingertip should point at the scaphoid.

OMT atlas — upper extremity

Spencer stages 1–2

Spencer stages 3–4

Spencer stage 5

Spencer stages 6–7

🔑 The Seven Stages of Spencer

She called this out by name — "we talked about the seven stages of Spencer... Spencer technique is to increase range of motion." Support the shoulder and block the scapula, then work through:

  1. ExtensionElbow flexed, arm extended.
  2. FlexionElbow extended, arm flexed forward.
  3. Circumduction with COMPRESSIONSmall-to-large circles with compression into the glenoid.
  4. Circumduction with TRACTIONSame circles, traction instead of compression.
  5. Abduction with external rotation(Often taught as adduction/ER — check your lab's version.)
  6. Internal rotationPatient's hand behind the back, gently lifted.
  7. Traction / stretch (abduction with traction)Pump the tissue with the arm abducted.

Key add-on she stressed: "You can take a Spencer technique and make it a muscle energy Spencer technique where you can have the person push back at you too." Add an isometric contraction at selected stages, 3–5 sec, repeat 3–5×, then recheck ROM.

🧠 Memory Hook — Spencer's seven

"Every Fine Circle Counts, Abduct, Internally, Traction" → Extension · Flexion · Circumduction+Compression · Circumduction+traction · Abduction/ER · Internal rotation · Traction/stretch.
Simpler: "2 straight, 2 circles, then AB-IR-TRACTION."

TechniqueUseRecipe
First rib BLT (supine)First rib / thoracic outlet / TOS / rib-clavicle mechanicsThumb on the posterosuperior first rib, fingers at the anterior first rib. Disengage posterior/anterior articulations, balance A-P / medial-lateral / superior-inferior, patient turns the head to the opposite side until T1 rotates away, then respiratory cooperation until release
Supine rib BLTRib dysfunction and thoracic-rib couplingFinger at the rib angle draws the rib head anterolaterally to disengage. Other hand stabilizes and pulls the spinous processes toward the physician to rotate the vertebra away. Breathing + hold until correction
Clavicle BLTSC/AC/clavicle dysfunction, TOS, shoulder girdle restrictionSeated, thumbs under the medial and lateral clavicle. Patient slouches/leans forward onto the thumbs while the physician resists and carries the shoulder posteriorly; the opposite shoulder retracts; balance the clavicle over the costoclavicular ligament with an inhalation hold
Scapulothoracic BLT/BMTScapula-rib, serratus/subscap/pec/lat, scapular dyskinesisThumbs enter the axillary space between scapula and ribs as the patient elevates then lowers the shoulder onto the contacts. Move the scapula through protraction/retraction, ab/adduction, elevation/depression; add humeral and breath cooperation
Glenohumeral BLTGH capsule restriction, IR/ER dysfunction, adhesive capsulitis supportGrasp the proximal humerus, gently disengage laterally; patient places a hand on the opposite shoulder and retracts to increase disengagement. Raise the elbow for an internal rotation dysfunction; depress the elbow for an external rotation dysfunction; hold until the strain resolves
Forearm interosseous membrane MFRDeep forearm restriction, pronation/supination dysfunction, nerve proximityGrasp radius and ulna as levers. Toggle A/P, superior/inferior, compression/distraction; hold barriers until release, moving distal to proximal
Carpal tunnel MFRCTS, flexor retinaculum restriction, venous/lymphatic congestionFingers on the posterior wrist, thenar eminences anterior over the transverse carpal ligament; gently spread/open it like a book, adding superior/inferior and compression/distraction. Patient slowly opens and closes the fingers
Wrist BLTGlobal wrist/carpal ligamentous imbalanceInterlace hands around the wrist, gently compress, carry through flex/ext and radial/ulnar deviation to balance. Patient spreads/extends the fingers maximally then relaxes
Carpal bone Still / FPRSpecific scaphoid/lunate/capitate restrictionMonitor the restricted carpal; use the metacarpal/thumb/finger as a lever. Still: ease → compression → corrective arc. FPR: compression + ease, short hold, return, recheck
Counterstrain — pectoralis minorAnterior chest/shoulder pain, rounded shoulder, pec minor/TOS contributionTender point inferior/medial to the coracoid. Supine, physician on the opposite side; move the arm diagonally across the chest and apply inferomedial compression to enhance scapular protraction. Hold 90 sec
Counterstrain — lateral radial headLateral epicondylitis / forearm painTender point lateral to the radial head near the supinator. Extend, supinate, and slightly abduct the forearm until tenderness improves; hold 90 seconds; slow return
Counterstrain — medial epicondyleMedial epicondylitis / pronator teres tendernessTender point at the proximal medial forearm at the pronator teres attachment. Flex, pronate, and slightly adduct until tenderness improves; hold 90 seconds; slow return
🧭 Lab flexibility — one contact, many techniques

The same forearm/carpal contacts become MFR, BLT, Still, FPR, or articulatory just by changing the force: direct/indirect barriers for MFR, a balanced midpoint for BLT, ease–compression–motion for Still, and compression + ease for FPR. If a stem describes the same hand placement twice with different forces, the technique name is the difference.

Q: A 55-year-old diabetic has months of shoulder pain that has become stiffness. Both active AND passive ROM are restricted, external rotation worst. Biceps tests, drop-arm, and painful arc are all negative, and you notice the scapula hiking early with abduction. Diagnosis, and what is the single highest-yield treatment technique?

Answer

Adhesive capsulitis. The tells: both active and passive restriction, the capsular pattern (ER > abduction > flexion), scapular substitution, and the conspicuous absence of biceps, drop-arm, crepitus, and painful-arc findings. Diabetes is a classic risk factor.
Highest-yield technique: the seven stages of Spencer, ideally converted to a muscle energy Spencer by having the patient push back at selected stages.

Q: A patient has median-distribution tingling, but Durkan, Phalen, and Tinel at the wrist are all negative. Pressure over the proximal forearm reproduces the symptoms. Diagnosis and treatment?

Answer

Pronator teres syndrome — median nerve entrapment under the pronator teres, not at the wrist. Treat with flexor/pronator MFR, interosseous membrane MFR/BLT/FPR, radial head/forearm mechanics, ergonomics, and PT.

Q: A 24-month-old is brought in after being lifted by the arm. She holds the elbow flexed and pronated and refuses to move it. Diagnosis, mechanism, and reduction maneuver?

Answer

Nursemaid's elbow — radial head subluxation from the annular ligament after axial traction, classically ages 12–35 months. Screen for fracture and neurovascular integrity first, then reduce with supination + flexion. Dr. Doan noted this specific question won't be on this exam but "it was on every one of my board exams" and returns in pediatrics.

Week 8 · LO 2
Week 2 · LO 7–8

"Explain, compare and contrast inhaled and exhaled rib dysfunction and treat them with muscle energy" ⭐ PROMISED

Ribs

🔑 Physiologic vs non-physiologic — do NOT mix the naming systems

An inhalation/exhalation dysfunction is respiratory physiology. An anterior/posterior rib subluxation is mechanical position. They are two different naming systems and the exam will try to blend them.

Physiologic (respiratory) rib dysfunction

⬆️

INHALATION dysfunction — "stuck UP"

  • The rib has greater excursion on inhalation but cannot move down
  • It rises with inhalation but will not return down with exhalation
  • Exhalation is the restricted motion
  • Named for the freedom: inhaled
  • KEY RIB = the BOTTOM rib of the group — treat it to pull the group down
⬇️

EXHALATION dysfunction — "stuck DOWN"

  • The rib goes down fine but doesn't like to come up
  • It is stuck down
  • Inhalation is the restricted motion
  • Named for the freedom: exhaled
  • KEY RIB = the TOP rib of the group — treat it to pull the group up
🧠 Memory Hook — the key rib (this is Savarese's "BITE")

B·I·T·E → Bottom rib for Inhalation dysfunction · Top rib for Exhalation dysfunction.
Reason it out if you blank: a group stuck UP needs to be pulled DOWN, so you grab the bottom one. A group stuck DOWN needs pulling UP, so you grab the top one. "Grab the end you want to pull toward."

Muscle energy for ribs — which muscle for which rib

"When you do muscle energy, what ribs are usually working? What muscles go with what ribs?" She warned that board questions sometimes shift the levels by one — you'll see serratus anterior listed as 6–9, for instance.

Rib(s)Muscle used for MENote
Rib 1Anterior and middle scalenePump-handle and bucket-handle motion. Also the TOS rib
Rib 2Posterior scalene—
Ribs 3–5Pectoralis minor—
Ribs 6–8Serratus anteriorSome sources say 6–9 — she flagged that boards mix it up
Ribs 9–10Latissimus dorsiSome sources shift this too
Ribs 11–12Quadratus lumborumCaliper motion
🧠 Memory Hook — rib ME muscles

"Some Silly People Sing Loud Quietly" →
Scalene ant/mid (1) · Scalene posterior (2) · Pectoralis minor (3–5) · Serratus anterior (6–8) · Latissimus dorsi (9–10) · Quadratus lumborum (11–12).
Numerically: 1, 2, 3-5, 6-8, 9-10, 11-12 — the pairs stay in order top to bottom.

Rib motion types

RibsMotionWhere to palpate
Rib 1Both pump-handle and bucket-handlePosterior first rib near the costotransverse area, plus the anterior rib under the clavicle. If it doesn't rise well on inhalation but exhales fully → exhaled
Ribs 2–5 (upper)Pump-handle — anterior/superior motionAnterior ribs. Assess inhalation/exhalation lag. Respect breast tissue and consent
Ribs 6–10Bucket-handle — lateral/superior motionLateral contacts toward the axilla; compare sides during breathing
Ribs 11–12Caliper — posterolateralPosterolateral caliper contact. If a side doesn't fully exhale, it's inhaled on that side
🧠 Memory Hook — motion types

"Pump on top, Bucket in the middle, Caliper at the bottom." Rib 1 does both pump and bucket. 11–12 are floating, so they swing like calipers.

Non-physiologic (mechanical) rib subluxation

Dr. Frothingham "mostly talked about anterior and posterior rib subluxation — make sure that you know how to identify them." Medial displacements and torsions were not covered in depth.

Anterior vs posterior mechanical rib subluxation

NamePosterior rib angleAnterior ribHow to confirm it's the same rib
Anterior rib subluxationDeep / less prominent posteriorlyProminent anteriorlyKeep a posterior finger on the rib angle and gently move front/back until both contacts move the same rib
Posterior rib subluxationProminent posterior rib angleDeep anteriorlyCompare with adjacent ribs and reproduce local tenderness at the same rib
🧠 Memory Hook — mechanical ribs

"The name tells you where it sticks out." Anterior rib = prominent in front, deep in back. Posterior rib = prominent in back, deep in front. Named by the freedom/position, same as everything else in OMM.

Still is the Week 2 treatment for these: monitor the rib angle, find ipsilateral arm ease, compress toward the rib, then move the arm through the opposite arc to the barrier.

⚠ The rib-vs-vertebra trap, one more time

Non-physiologic ribs are usually from trauma and have sharp, discrete "ice-pick" pain. If there's no trauma, check the adjacent thoracic vertebra first — a posterior rib angle may simply be following a rotated vertebra through the costotransverse ligament, and treating the vertebra makes the "rib" disappear.

Q: Ribs 4, 5, and 6 on the right rise well with inhalation but do not descend fully with exhalation. Name the dysfunction, identify the key rib, and name the muscle you would use for muscle energy.

Answer

Right ribs 4–6 inhalation dysfunction (stuck up; exhalation restricted). By BITE, the key rib is the BOTTOM rib of the group — rib 6. Rib 6 is served by the serratus anterior, so that's the muscle the patient contracts against your resistance. (If the key rib had been rib 5, it would be pectoralis minor.)

Q: Ribs 2–4 on the left will not rise with inhalation. Key rib and muscle?

Answer

Left ribs 2–4 exhalation dysfunction (stuck down; inhalation restricted). By BITE, the key rib is the TOP rib — rib 2 — treated with the posterior scalene.

Week 8 · Innominates + Sacrum
Week 1 · LO 2, 4

"You'll have to know how to identify an innominate diagnosis based on case findings" ⭐ PROMISED

Pelvis & Sacrum

She flagged two separate promised items here: innominate diagnosis from case findings (including standing flexion, ASIS compression tests) and diagnosing a forward or backward sacral torsion from a case vignette.

Innominate diagnosis

DiagnosisASISPSISPubic tubercleExtra
Anterior innominateInferiorSuperiorInferiorSame side throughout — the whole innominate rotated forward
Posterior innominateSuperiorInferiorSuperiorThe mirror image
OutflareMore lateral from midline—More anteriorWing flares out
InflareCloser to midline—More posteriorWing flares in
Superior / inferior shearASIS, PSIS, and pubic tubercle ALL shift superior or inferior togetherEverything moves the same direction — that's the tell
🧠 Memory Hook — innominate rotation

"ANTERIOR = ASIS goes down, PSIS goes up." Picture the innominate as a wheel rotating forward: the front point dips, the back point lifts. Pubic tubercle follows the ASIS (both are front structures).
"SHEAR = everything agrees." If all three landmarks are on the same side of the fence (all up or all down), it's a shear, not a rotation.

Standing vs seated flexion test

TestWhat it tells youWhich side is positivePractical pitfall
Standing flexion testInnominate / iliosacral lateralityThe side where the PSIS moves first and farthest = the restricted / dysfunctional side (same side)Hook under the inferior PSIS and keep fingers on the iliac crest; the patient must fully flex
Seated flexion testSacroiliac / sacral laterality — an axis clueThe PSIS that moves first and farthest tells you which side is stuck. Whatever goes up, the OPPOSITE side is the axis of the torsionFeet must be on the floor. Same inferior PSIS contact. Bilateral sacral flexion or extension can produce a FALSE NEGATIVE — she flagged this specifically
Supine ASIS + pubic tuberclesAnterior/posterior innominate, shears, in/out flares—Reseat the pelvis first; consent before pubic contact; approach from the abdomen down to the pubis
ASIS compression testRight vs left SI restrictionThe restricted sideForce is posterior-medial, following the SI joint orientation — not straight down

Sacral diagnosis

🧭 The three findings that build a sacral diagnosis
  1. Which sacral sulcus is DEEP?Go medial to the PSIS to find the sulcus.
  2. Which ILA is posterior/inferior?Compare the inferior lateral angles for posterior and inferior asymmetry.
  3. Seated flexion testGives the side, and therefore the axis (opposite side).
  4. Spring test and/or SphinxSeparates forward from backward mechanics.
TestHowPositiveMeaning
Spring test
Also: lumbosacral spring test		Spring on the sacral basePOSITIVE = does NOT springPositive → backward / extended / posterior sacral base = BACKWARD torsion. Negative (it springs) → forward sacral base = FORWARD torsion
Sphinx test
Also called the prone press-up or backward bending test — boards may say "prone press-up"		Prone, thumbs in the sacral sulci. Patient props up on their elbows, extending the lumbar spineSulci become MORE symmetric (thumbs come closer together) → FORWARD torsion. Sulci become MORE asymmetric (thumbs separate further) → BACKWARD torsionExtension improves a forward torsion and worsens a backward one
L5 relationshipDiagnose L5—L5 is rotated OPPOSITE the sacrum (usually)
DiagnosisDeep sulcusPosterior/inferior ILASeated flexion test +Spring / Sphinx
L on L (forward)LeftRightRightSpring negative · Sphinx improves
R on R (forward)RightLeftLeftSpring negative · Sphinx improves
L on R (backward)RightLeftLeftSpring positive · Sphinx worsens
R on L (backward)LeftRightRightSpring positive · Sphinx worsens
🧠 Memory Hook — forward vs backward torsion

"SAME letters = FORWARD. DIFFERENT letters = BACKWARD." L on L and R on R are forward torsions; L on R and R on L are backward. That single rule sorts half the question.
"Sphinx tests EXTENSION, and extension LIKES a forward torsion." If propping up makes the sulci even out → forward. If it makes them worse → backward.
"Positive spring = NO spring = Backward." Positive sounds like "good" but here it means the base won't move — it's already back.

🔑 The conflict rule

Week 1's lecture pearl: when the seated flexion test conflicts with the spring/sphinx findings, default to spring/sphinx — they are more specific for forward vs backward torsion. And remember: bilateral sacral flexion or extension gives a false-negative seated flexion test, so if the seated flexion test is negative but everything else is asymmetric, look for a bilateral diagnosis.

Q: Left sacral sulcus deep, right ILA posterior and inferior, seated flexion test positive on the right, spring test negative, and the sphinx test improves symmetry. Name the sacral diagnosis.

Answer

Left-on-left sacral torsion (L on L) — a forward torsion on a left oblique axis. Check every finding: deep sulcus left, posterior ILA right, seated flexion positive right (so the axis is the opposite side — left), and both negative spring and an improving sphinx confirm forward mechanics. And by the same-letters rule, "L on L" is forward.

Q: Standing flexion test is positive on the right. The right ASIS is inferior, the right pubic tubercle is inferior, and the right PSIS is superior. Name it.

Answer

Anterior right innominate. Standing flexion gives the side; then ASIS down + pubic tubercle down + PSIS up is exactly anterior rotation. If all three landmarks had moved the same direction, it would be a shear instead.

Week 8 · review slides
Nicholas & Nicholas

"Intermixed between the weeks" — Dr. Bissette, Dr. Smilowicz, Dr. Doan, Dr. Stevens, Dr. Yi

Counterstrain Review

She added a block of counterstrain slides at the end "just in case" — cervical, the rest of the spine, and ribs — noting these are the rules, drawn from the Nicholas & Nicholas OMT review book, one of the books on the course list.

🔑 The counterstrain recipe, exactly as she gave it
  1. Find the MOST tender pointNot "a" tender point — the worst one.
  2. Keep your palpating finger on itYou must monitor the same point the entire time and at recheck.
  3. Establish a 0–10 tenderness scaleSet the baseline at 10/10 by definition, then position.
  4. Position into ease until tenderness drops to ≤3/10You need at least a 70% reduction before you settle in.
  5. Hold 90 secondsAlways 90 for a peripheral/spinal point.
  6. PASSIVE slow return to neutral"The patient does not help you go to neutral — you'll help the patient to neutral." Patient assistance ruins the treatment.
  7. Recheck the same pointIdeally 0/10 or near it, with resolved tissue texture change.
🧠 Memory Hook — counterstrain

"Find it, Fold it, 90, Float them back." Find the worst tender point, fold the patient into ease until it drops to ≤3/10, hold 90 seconds, then you float them back to neutral — passively.
The two most-missed points: "Finger never leaves the point" and "the return must be PASSIVE."

Positioning rules by point location

Point groupPosition of easeRule of thumb
Anterior points (general)FLEX toward the pointAnterior tender points want flexion. Fold the patient around the point
Posterior points (general)EXTEND away from the pointPosterior tender points want extension
Anterior cervical AC2–AC6Flex to the segment, then sidebend AWAY and rotate AWAY from the tender pointSARA — Sidebend Away, Rotate Away
Anterior lumbar AL3 / AL4Around the AIIS. Flex the hips to the level, sidebend and rotate awayTender point location drives the position of comfort
Anterior lumbar AL5Near the pubic ramus. Marked hip flexion, rotate toward, sidebend awayAL5 breaks the pattern — rotation is toward
Psoas tender pointMarked hip flexion, knees flexed, ankles crossed, hips externally rotated, slight ipsilateral sidebendingPoint is medial to the ASIS. Presents as anterior hip/thigh or thoracolumbar pain with reduced hip extension
Piriformis tender pointProne; hip flexed to ~90° and markedly abducted; fine-tune rotationPoint is midway between the greater trochanter and the coccyx/PSIS line
Lateral hamstring (biceps femoris)Prone; markedly flex the knee, externally rotate the tibia on the femurPoint just below the ischial tuberosity, or ~1/3 above the distal fibular-head attachment
Medial hamstringProne; markedly flex the knee, internally rotate the tibia on the femurSemimembranosus/semitendinosus
Pectoralis minorSupine; move the arm diagonally across the chest with inferomedial compression to protract the scapulaPoint is inferior/medial to the coracoid
Lateral radial head (lateral epicondylitis)Extend, supinate, slightly abduct the forearmPoint lateral to the radial head near the supinator
Medial epicondyle (medial epicondylitis)Flex, pronate, slightly adduct the forearmPoint at the proximal medial forearm at the pronator teres attachment
🧠 Memory Hook — the counterstrain direction logic

"Shorten the muscle the point lives in." Every position of ease slackens the tissue holding the tender point. Lateral epicondyle = extensors/supinators → you extend and supinate. Medial epicondyle = flexors/pronators → you flex and pronate. Lateral hamstring inserts laterally → externally rotate. It's the same idea every time.

Q: A physician finds a tender point, positions the patient until tenderness drops from 10/10 to 2/10, holds 90 seconds, then asks the patient to sit themselves back up. What went wrong?

Answer

The return to neutral must be PASSIVE — the physician moves the patient. Active patient movement on the return re-engages the muscle spindles and can undo the treatment. Dr. Doan said it plainly: "The patient does not help you go to neutral; you'll help the patient to neutral."

Week 3 · LO 11
Week 5 & 7

"When do you get an MRI?" — she walked this out loud

Imaging & Diagnostic Studies

🧠 Memory Hook — the whole imaging decision in one line

"HARD → CT/X-ray. SOFT → MRI. SIGNAL → EMG."
Bone problem? X-ray or CT. Ligament, labrum, meniscus, disc, or cord? MRI. Nerve function? EMG/NCS.

StudyBest useHer specific examples
X-rayTrauma, suspected fracture, alignment, degeneration overview, instability screeningOttawa ankle/knee positive. Boxer's fracture. Gamekeeper's thumb before the stress test. Zanca view for the AC joint. Flexion-extension views for dynamic instability; oblique views for foraminal narrowing and the Scotty dog
CTBone detail, acute trauma, complex/occult fracture, when MRI is unavailable or contraindicated"If you think it's a fracture, you'll get a CAT scan." Acute intracranial bleed. Old strokes
MRI (no contrast)Soft tissue: disc herniation, stenosis, nerve root compression, myelopathy, ligament/tendon/labrum/meniscus, cartilage"Meniscal tears — MRI is better than ultrasound because it's soft and it's in a joint." Labral tear of shoulder or hip. Herniated disc. Acute stroke. Rotator cuff tear
MRI with contrastSuspected cancer/infection, postoperative scar vs recurrent disc, inflammatory/mass processUse contrast if cancer is on the differential or there's a history of prior spinal surgery
MR arthrogramLabrum and intra-articular pathology — contrast injected into the jointSLAP/labral tear of the shoulder ("you might even do an arthrogram that adds contrast"); hip labral tear
CT myelogramWhen MRI is contraindicated or equivocalDye cutoff/blunting identifies the affected root sleeve
UltrasoundDynamic tendon assessment, guided injections, soft-tissue masses, abdominal organsBiceps tendon in the bicipital groove; US-guided AC injection; UCL thumb; tendon retraction in jersey finger; Baker cyst; abdomen/gallbladder
EMG / NCSNerve conduction — the functional testGOLD STANDARD for carpal tunnel syndrome and for significant ulnar neuropathy. Also distinguishes a root lesion from a peripheral neuropathy. "It's a nerve conduction test... and it's painful"
Labs / aspirationInflammatory, infectious, crystal, endocrine, systemic diseaseSeptic olecranon bursitis aspiration (gold standard); diabetes/thyroid/rheum workup when adhesive capsulitis has no obvious driver
⚠ Do NOT confuse these three
  • EMG (electromyogram / nerve conduction study) = nerve and muscle. Gold standard for carpal tunnel.
  • EEG (electroencephalogram) = brain waves.
  • Echocardiogram = heart, using ultrasound (with venous Doppler for chambers/flow).

She spelled this out explicitly because the distractors are obvious once you've seen them.

🔑 Do NOT image every radiculopathy immediately

For uncomplicated acute low back pain or radiculopathy without red flags, guidelines avoid immediate imaging. Image early only for red flags, progressive neurologic deficit, or when symptoms persist despite conservative care and an injection/surgical pathway is being considered. And remember: degenerative findings are extremely common in asymptomatic people — clinical correlation is mandatory.

The corollary she gave for management: avoid prolonged bed rest — "bed rest over 2 days is bad." Education and staying active win.

🧠 Memory Hook — CT vs MRI for stroke & bleeds

"Fresh Blood → CT. Fresh Stroke → MRI. Old Stroke → CT." Acute bleeds show up on CT; acute ischemic strokes need MRI; old infarcts are visible on CT.

Q: A patient has classic nocturnal median-distribution numbness and a positive Durkan test. Surgery is being considered. What study confirms the diagnosis, and what does it measure?

Answer

EMG / nerve conduction study — the gold standard for carpal tunnel syndrome. It stimulates the nerve and measures conduction velocity and latency across the involved segment. Do not confuse it with EEG (brain waves) or echocardiogram (heart).

Q: A basketball player has a locked knee after a loaded twist, with medial joint-line pain. Which imaging study, and why not ultrasound?

Answer

MRI. Her reasoning verbatim: the meniscus is soft tissue inside a joint — MRI sees it far better than ultrasound. A truly locked knee also goes to orthopedics rather than to forceful OMT.

Active recall

Say the answer out loud before you reveal

Rapid Fire

Q: Name every technique she said is indirect and passive.

Answer

Counterstrain and FPR. That's the whole list. Everything else is either direct, or capable of being both.

Q: How long do you hold: FPR? Counterstrain? MFR? A muscle energy contraction?

Answer

FPR 3–5 sec · Counterstrain 90 sec · MFR 20–60 sec, usually 30–60 · ME contraction 3–5 sec, repeated 3–5 times. Still has no hold. BLT waits for release: ~10 sec for a response, 20–30+ for completion.

Q: Which technique cannot be used on a patient with dementia, and why?

Answer

Muscle energy — it's the only active technique, so it requires the patient to follow directions and contract on command. Same reason it's out for young children and cognitive delay.

Q: A group of thoracic vertebrae is neutral, sidebent left, rotated right. Which segment do you treat?

Answer

The middle of the group. Type I dysfunctions are group curves and you treat the apex/middle — she said this explicitly.

Q: A patient has neck pain, hand clumsiness, brisk reflexes, positive Hoffman, and an unsteady gait. What is this, and can you do cervical HVLA?

Answer

Myelopathy — upper motor neuron signs mean possible cord compression. No HVLA. Escalate to urgent MRI and specialty evaluation. This is a contraindication to aggressive OMT, not a segmental problem.

Q: What are the four absolute contraindications to OMM?

Answer

Lack of consent · inability to participate or follow directions · treatment over an open wound or sutured area · instability of the bony architecture. Everything else on the danger list — fracture, dislocation, neurologic or vascular compromise, malignancy, infection, bleeding — is relative.

Q: Which region do you treat first when you have a choice, and why?

Answer

The thoracic inlet / outlet, usually with BLT or MFR — you open the drainage system first so that treating the head lets things drain down and treating the body lets things drain up.

Q: A patient has a "posterior rib" on screening but no trauma history. What do you check before diagnosing a mechanical rib?

Answer

The adjacent thoracic vertebra. A rotated vertebra drags the rib posteriorly through the costotransverse ligament. Treat the thoracic segment and the "posterior rib" often resolves. True mechanical rib dysfunction usually follows trauma and has sharp, discrete "ice-pick" pain.

Q: Positive spring test on the sacral base. Forward or backward torsion?

Answer

Backward. "Positive" means it does not spring — the sacral base is already backward/extended/posterior. A negative spring test (it springs freely) means a forward sacral base and a forward torsion.

Q: Patient can't extend the DIP after a ball hit the fingertip. Diagnosis and treatment?

Answer

Mallet finger — extensor tendon rupture at the DIP. Splint the DIP in extension for 6 weeks unless there's a large articular avulsion or the joint is unstable, which goes to surgery. (Its mirror, jersey finger, is a loss of DIP flexion from FDP avulsion and needs early surgery.)

Q: What is the gold standard test to prove carpal tunnel syndrome, and what test does the exam most want to distinguish it from?

Answer

EMG / nerve conduction study. Distinguish it from EEG (brain waves) and echocardiogram (heart) — Dr. Doan called all three out in the same breath because the distractors write themselves.

Q: Which cervical root is most commonly compressed, and what is the most common cause of cervical root compression symptoms overall?

Answer

Root: C7 (~70%), then C6 (~20%). Most common cause overall: spondylosis — degenerative DJD change. "Osis is old."

Q: Where exactly is the psoas tender point, and what is the counterstrain position?

Answer

Point: medial to the ASIS. Position: marked hip flexion, knees flexed, ankles crossed, hips externally rotated, with slight ipsilateral sidebending. Hold 90 seconds, passive return.

Q: Which nerve is injured in scapular winging, which muscle fails, and how do you demonstrate it?

Answer

Long thoracic nerve injury → serratus anterior weakness. The scapula protrudes posteromedially when the patient pushes against a wall.

Q: A patient's leg pain travels farther down the leg during your lumbar treatment. What do you do?

Answer

Stop or modify immediately. Peripheralization means the position or force is wrong. Reassess the neurologic exam and the diagnosis. Prefer positions that centralize symptoms.

🎯 OMM Written Exam — High-Yield One-Pager

Weeks 1–8 · everything Dr. Doan promised would be on the exam, compressed. Print this the night before.

5 Osteopathic Models — "Big Rusty Nails Move Bones"

  • Biomechanical: posture, motion, gait, alignment
  • Respiratory/Circulatory: arteries, veins, lymph, diffusion, edema, breathing
  • Neurologic: autonomics, facilitation, neuroendocrine-immune. Rib raising = neurologic (↓ sympathetic tone)
  • Metabolic/Energetic: efficiency, energy conservation
  • Behavioral: psychosocial, education, coping, lifestyle

TART — "Acute = Angry & Wet · Chronic = Cold & Ropey"

AcuteChronic
TissueErythema, boggy, moist, warm, hypertonic, spasmPale, cool, dry, flaccid, ropey, fibrotic, ↓ tone
AsymmetryPresentPresent, partially compensated
RestrictionPresent, painful w/ motionPresent but decreased
TendernessSharp, severeDull, achy, minimal

Barriers — "PEA in a pod"

  • Physiologic: limit of ACTIVE motion
  • Elastic: the passive range the physician can access
  • Anatomic: limit of PASSIVE motion; beyond = tissue/joint disruption. Never a target
  • Restrictive/pathologic: a functional limit within normal active ROM. Direct engages it; indirect moves away. Can become permanent
  • Neutral/idling: facets neither open nor closed = FPR's start

Fryette — "1 = N-O-G · 2 = two S's"

  • Type I: Neutral · sidebending & rotation Opposite · Group. Treat the middle of the group
  • Type II: Non-neutral (F or E) · S & R Same side · Single segment
  • Type III: Newton — motion in one plane reduces motion in the others
  • Always named for the FREEDOM of motion
  • OA = Opposite Always · AA = rotation only, test at 45° · C2–C7 = same side (joints of Luschka)

Selection, Sequencing & Safety

  • Sequence: thoracic inlet/outlet FIRST (BLT/MFR) → thoracic BEFORE ribs → lumbar/cervical → axial before extremities (unless a spasm needs it first)
  • Older patients → indirect, unless very sick. More frequent tx if acute and in children; fewer areas if unhealthy
  • No ME if the patient can't follow directions (kids, dementia, cognitive delay)
  • No direct techniques with growth/bony compromise, osteoporosis at the joint, or Down syndrome (⭐ HY — atlantoaxial instability)
  • ABSOLUTE CI: no consent · can't participate/follow directions · over open wound or sutures · bony instability
  • RELATIVE CI: dislocation, fracture, neurologic compromise, vascular compromise, malignancy/metastasis, infection, bleeding

Ribs — BITE

  • Inhalation dysfunction: stuck UP, won't come down → KEY = BOTTOM rib
  • Exhalation dysfunction: stuck DOWN, won't come up → KEY = TOP rib
  • ME muscles "Some Silly People Sing Loud Quietly": 1 = ant/mid scalene · 2 = post scalene · 3–5 = pec minor · 6–8 = serratus ant · 9–10 = lats · 11–12 = QL
  • Motion: pump-handle 1–5 · bucket-handle 6–10 · caliper 11–12 (rib 1 does both pump & bucket)
  • Mechanical: anterior rib = prominent front/deep back · posterior rib = prominent back/deep front. Check the thoracic vertebra first

Sacrum & Innominates

  • Standing flexion = innominate/iliosacral, positive on the same side
  • Seated flexion = sacral; PSIS first & farthest; axis is the OPPOSITE side. Feet on floor. Bilateral flexion/extension → false negative
  • Spring test POSITIVE = does NOT spring = BACKWARD torsion. Negative = forward
  • Sphinx (prone press-up / backward bending): sulci more symmetric = FORWARD; thumbs separate = backward
  • SAME letters (L on L, R on R) = FORWARD · different = backward
  • L5 rotates opposite the sacrum. When seated flexion conflicts, trust spring/sphinx
  • Anterior innominate: ASIS ↓, PSIS ↑, pubic tubercle ↓. Shear: all three move together

Radiculopathy Essentials

  • C7 (~70%) > C6 (~20%) · lumbar: L5 & S1. Reflexes: biceps C5–6, brachioradialis C6, triceps C7, patellar L4, Achilles S1
  • Radiculitis = pain/paresthesia only · Radiculopathy = objective deficit · Myelopathy = UMN/cord
  • Cord tests (L-H-C-B): Lhermitte, Hoffman, Clonus, Babinski → urgent MRI, no HVLA
  • Spurling: turn the head TOWARD the pain + axial compression. SLR: 30–70°, pain below knee; crossed SLR more specific
  • Cauda equina (S-B-B): Saddle anesthesia, Bowel/Bladder, Bilateral. Same-day emergency
  • 8 cervical roots: upper 7 exit above their vertebra, C8 below C7. Brachial plexus C5–T1. Cord ends L1–L2. L4 exits between L4/L5
  • Peripheralization = stop. Prefer centralizing positions

The Spondylo Family & Stenosis vs Disc

  • Lysis = Loss of pars (Scotty dog collar, classically L5)
  • Listhesis = Lets go/slides (step-off; isthmic L5–S1, degenerative L4–L5)
  • Osis = Old (degenerative DJD — most common cause of cervical root compression symptoms)
  • Arthropathy = Autoimmune (morning stiffness better with exercise, alternating buttock pain, HLA-B27)
  • CART = CANAL: Stenosis worse upright/extension, better leaning forward. Disc worse with flexion/sitting/cough. Posterolateral herniation at L4–L5, L5–S1, L3–L4

Psoas & Piriformis

  • Psoas syndrome: iliopsoas spasm (flexion contracture) · positive Thomas test · tender point medial to ASIS · non-neutral L1–L2 SAME side · pelvic side shift CONTRALATERAL · sacral oblique-axis dysfunction · contralateral piriformis spasm
  • Piriformis syndrome: sciatic nerve under the piriformis → posterolateral leg symptoms, worse sitting. Congenital, traumatic, or somatic dysfunction
  • Sciatica = low back/buttock → posterolateral thigh → foot, roots L4–S3. A distribution, not a diagnosis
  • CS positions: psoas = marked hip flexion, knees flexed, ankles crossed, hips ER. Piriformis = prone, hip flexed ~90° and markedly abducted

Lower Extremity

  • Gait: heel strike (tib ant eccentric) → foot flat (arch absorbs) → heel off (gastroc-soleus concentric) → pre-swing (windlass)
  • Ottawa ANKLE: bone tenderness at posterior edge/tip of either malleolus, navicular, or base of 5th MT, or can't bear weight 4 steps
  • Ottawa KNEE: age ≥55, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, can't flex 90°, can't bear weight 4 steps
  • Sprains: I = stretch, no instability · II = incomplete tear (ATFL), pain walking, mild instability, severe swelling · III = complete tear (ATFL+CFL), can't bear weight, mechanical instability. Lateral > medial (deltoid is stronger)
  • Terrible triad (A-M-M): ACL + MCL + medial meniscus
  • PA/SP: Pronation → fibular head Anterior; Supination → Posterior. Proximal and distal always opposite. Tibia ER with knee extension + posterolateral glide
  • Morton neuroma: toes 3–4, tight shoes, Mulder click, transverse arch collapse. Foot drop: fibular head or L5
  • Meralgia paresthetica: LFCN, sensory-only anterolateral thigh. Any weakness → not meralgia

Upper Extremity

  • Entrapments: CUBital = eLBow, Guyon = wrist (both ulnar, digits 4–5, both mimicked by C8). CTS = median under transverse carpal ligament, digits 1–3 + radial ½ of 4, nocturnal. Durkan best exam test; EMG/NCS gold standard. Pronator teres = CTS mimic with proximal forearm symptoms
  • Radial nerve = most common UE nerve injury, direct trauma → wrist drop + weak triceps
  • TOS: brachial plexus + subclavian vessels at scalenes/first rib/clavicle/pec minor. Adson's test
  • Cuff: SITS · painful arc 60–120° · empty can & drop arm = supraspinatus · lift-off = subscapularis · Neer/Hawkins = impingement
  • Adhesive capsulitis: active AND passive restricted; E-A-F (ER worst → abduction → flexion); scapular substitution; negative biceps/drop-arm/crepitus/arc. Spencer (± ME) is HY
  • LET/MF: Lateral = Extensors/supinators = Tennis, worse w/ wrist extension. Medial = Flexors/pronators = golf, worse w/ wrist flexion. Both → counterstrain + MFR
  • Fall Forward = Pronated = Posterior radial head. Anterior head = restricted pronation (you pronate, they supinate); posterior = restricted supination
  • Nursemaid's: annular ligament, 12–35 months, axial traction; reduce with supination-flexion
  • JERSEY can't FLEX (FDP avulsion → early surgery) · MALLET can't EXTEND (splint in extension 6 wks)
  • Gamekeeper's: UCL of 1st MCP; x-ray BEFORE stress test; >35° laxity or no endpoint = rupture; grade 3 surgery within 21 days. Boxer's: 5th MC, check rotation, ulnar gutter splint

MFR & Soft Tissue · Fascia

  • MFR: direct or indirect, active or passive, targets the fascia, continuous palpatory feedback, unwinding, 30–60 sec
  • Soft tissue: direct + passive ONLY, goes deeper than fascia into muscle, linear/longitudinal stretch. Mechanism: ↓ alpha motor neuron activity
  • Connective tissue = the family · fascia = the continuous investing network · myofascia = fascia on muscle
  • Layers P-I-M-V: Pannicular, Investing, Meningeal (dura), Visceral
  • Functions PT SPAM: Protection/packing · Transmission of fluids · Structural support/locomotion · Proprioception/nociception · Adaptation/postural control · Mechanotransduction · Metabolic-immune
  • Terms: ease vs bind · creep (slow deformation under sustained low load) · hysteresis (energy lost as heat) · tensegrity (continuous tension in fascia, discontinuous compression in bone)
  • Both: remove restriction, restore homeostasis, ↑ circulation, ↑ immune response, augment ANS, relax

Counterstrain — "Find it, Fold it, 90, Float them back"

  • Most tender point → finger never leaves it → 0–10 scale → position of ease to ≤3/10 → 90 sec → PASSIVE return → recheck
  • Anterior points → flex. Posterior points → extend
  • AC2–AC6 = SARA: Sidebend Away, Rotate Away
  • AL5: marked hip flexion, rotate toward, sidebend away (breaks the pattern)
  • Lateral hamstring → knee flexion + ER of tibia. Medial → knee flexion + IR
  • Lateral epicondyle → extend + supinate. Medial epicondyle → flex + pronate. Shorten the muscle the point lives in

Imaging — "HARD → CT · SOFT → MRI · SIGNAL → EMG"

  • X-ray: trauma, fracture, alignment, Ottawa positive, Scotty dog (oblique), Zanca (AC), gamekeeper before stress test
  • CT: bone detail, complex/occult fracture, acute bleed, old stroke
  • MRI: disc, stenosis, cord/myelopathy, meniscus, labrum, rotator cuff, acute stroke. Contrast if cancer on DDx or prior spine surgery
  • MR arthrogram: labrum (shoulder SLAP, hip)
  • Ultrasound: biceps tendon in groove, guided injections, Baker cyst, abdomen
  • EMG/NCS: gold standard for CTS and ulnar neuropathy. Not EEG (brain waves), not echo (heart)
  • Don't image uncomplicated acute radiculopathy without red flags. Avoid bed rest >2 days

Red Flags (immediate attention)

  • Saddle anesthesia · bowel/bladder dysfunction · bilateral severe symptoms
  • Progressive neurologic deficit · asymmetric weakness · muscular atrophy · can't heel-toe walk · can't squat and stand
  • UMN/myelopathy signs: gait change, spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, Babinski, Hoffman, Lhermitte, fine-motor decline
  • Fever · weight loss · night/rest pain not relieved by any position · history of cancer · immunocompromise · IV drug use
  • Age >50 · rapid progression · significant trauma · step-off deformity · focal vertebral tenderness
  • Associated abdominal pain · dyspnea · vascular symptoms

Exam Blueprint

  • 115 questions. ~56 OMM-tagged, ~64 clinical-skills-tagged (some double-tagged)
  • Weeks 1–7 balanced. Week 8 #1 (diagnosis + techniques) overlaps everything → most questions
  • Written pass = 70% overall AND 70% on each half. Below 70% overall → retake the whole test (caps at 70%). Half below 70% → retake that half, grade unchanged
  • Course pass = 75%. Practical/skills/CSA = 75%
  • Written #1 = 15% · Written #2 = 25% (verify weights in the syllabus)
  • Explicitly promised questions: TART acute/chronic · barriers · Fryette Type I/II · inhaled vs exhaled ribs + ME · the 5 models · innominate diagnosis · forward vs backward sacral torsion
